SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Performing Arts
L'Enfant Plaza
Amtrak Building

J. C. Higginbotham
Side 1, Reels 1 & 2
J. C., why do they always have you born in Atlanta? Were you actually born in Atlanta?
No, I wasn't born in Atlanta.
I know. Everywhere they have you born in Atlanta, Georgia.
I know that. I was born 60 miles east of Atlanta, Social Circle.
Social Circle?
Social Circle, yeah. Down on the farm. ...
What year were you born?
Nineteen hundred and six.
What day?
May the 11th.
Just for the information, what was your mother's first name, your mother and father's name?
My mother's name TEMPIE, my father's name Charles.
When did you begin playing the trombone?

Oh, I think I was about probably 14. My brother was teaching at Morris Brown College. Well, I had moved from Georgia then, from Social Circle. We were living in Decatur like, you know, New York and Brooklyn. So, he was teaching tailoring and he bought a trombone. So I snuck up a couple of notes on it and I liked it and told my sister to buy me one. So she did. The guy delivered it that night about 8 o'clock. No case. The next morning I had the kids out in the backyard dancing in their bare feet. I never had no any lessons.
You never had any lessons? Just taught yourself?
Yes.
So your brother was teaching tailoring at Morris Brown College and Decatur is just outside of Atlanta. So it was because of his having a trombone that you got ...

I just happened to pick it up and liked it and kept on playing it. I was playing bugle before that. I paid played a dollar for a bugle and I played tunes on the bugle with my aunt. That was when I was going to church ... a man in a restaurant, I gave him a dollar for it. I was playing tunes ... no valves, no nothing. GAMES Used your hands ...
How long was it before you started working, I mean, even as a youngster, say at 14, how long was it before you started playing say around Atlanta and in that area?
Well, I did, say, my brother was teaching and he put me in that boarding school in Atlanta and I played there. I played in the band in college.
What was the name of the boarding school?
Morris Brown College.
Oh, Morris Brown?
Yeah, right. I stayed there.
Yeah, that's a famous school now.
Yeah, and I played and still couldn't read a note.
Well, when did you start learning to read?

He had me learning ... and the first tune was 'Poet and Peasant' ... every trombone player. So I'm looking at the music and he got up, stand up and walk around and he went on in this ear and planted the note and I'm watching the positions on the trombones.
You're watching the other trombone players?
Always eyes goin', that's why they so messed up now. other guy's positions are. So,
That's the way I started professionally. My brother wouldn't let me finish tailoring ...
You don't have to hold it. We've got mikes all around.

OK. So, I went to Cincinnati and while I was there I went to night school to finish tailoring and I worked in Wesley Helvey's band ... good band. he had a heck of a good band, still couldn't read the music. Wesley, how do you spell that last name?
H-e-l-v-e-y, Wesley, OK.
OK.
... played in his band a couple of nights a week, Did a whole lot of work go to night school for tailoring and worked at the Giant Motor Company in the morning.
Which one was that company?
Jenning Motor?
Jenning Motor?
Yeah, right. ...
Were all of these bands your friends around Atlanta?
No, no. I went from Cincinnati ... up here. Wingy (2) Carpenter, I don't know if you know him, trumpet player. The name is Theodore Carpenter.
Theodore Carpenter?

Right. I met him in Cincinnati and he was playing on the band there so he came to Buffalo and he sent for me to come to Buffalo, New York so I played there for about a little over a year. I played with Jim Harrison's band there, a piano player and Eugene Promise MN.
Jimmy Harrison a piano player?
Yeah. No, not the trombone player. No, lots of people get it mixed up. No, he played piano. But there was,
Was there a Jimmy Harrison trombone player?
Oh, yes and how ... listened to him all the time ...
Now when did you go to Cincinnati?
I went to Cincinnati twice. The last time I went there I think it was in 1924.
When was the first time?
Yeah.
Now did you leave specifically to join a band or something like that?
Yes, I did. In 1924 I went to Buffalo, New York.
Right.
A guy sent for me, this trumpet player ... used to play in church. Theodore Carpenter (both talking)
Yeah, I read that in one of the history books. He worked in Buffalo up there.
This was in 1928, September 8, 1928. You weren't even born.
Way before my time. How much playing did you do around Atlanta and Decatur and that area?
How much work?
Yeah.
Oh, I did quite a bit of work while I was there. Yeah, I was in school and we had a band there. Merrill Mayer Hamilton and they called it the Hamilton and Montgomery band.
Hamilton and Montgomery band?
Hamilton and Montgomery, Neil Montgomery and Merrill Hamilton. I played there for quite a while.
Who were some of your earliest influences. I mean, first of all, how did you get introduced to jazz?
In Atlanta?
Right.

Oh, my brother took me in the boarding school so ... I still had a horn and you had to stay on on Saturday night and you had to spend the night when you go in ... so I used to sneak out of the dormitory and go out and play at night and my brother would let me in. And then I got permission and we played quite a bit. And they played a lot of money, too.
What do you mean a lot of money, how much?
At the time about $5 or $10 a night was a lot of money, I'm telling you.
But, what made you decide to play jazz instead of playing poets or peasant or being...
I don't know. I just felt like playing jazz all of my life.
Well, what was one of the earliest trombonists that you listened to or trumpet player or somebody ...
I knew that was coming. I never had nobody to influence me, never.
Well, who were some of your favorites that you listened to in that period?

Jazz people, OWENS - Yeah, well, I didn't have no special people, I used to go listen to Jimmy Harrison. I said I was as good as they were. (... playing the horn ...) because practically every night, you know, that's when these places would stay open all night and we'd get through playing -- we'd play until 4 o'clock in the morning. Sometimes you'd play up until the next day ... sit back and drink your bottle, get high and blow your horn.
What were you playing? I mean, what kind of songs? Do you remember some of the songs?
Any kind, don't make no difference. All the jazz music.
Something like Louis Armstrong's compositions, things that he was playing?
Yeah.
What year was this about?
(inaudible) what?
I know, what year was this around in Atlanta or where you were doing all of this?
In Atlanta?
Yeah.
Well, that was in 1924, '23 and '24, when I was playing there because I left late in 1924.
Now, had you heard King Oliver's band, because they made some first recordings?
The first record I made was for him.
Oh, really?
1928 right here in New York but he couldn't play. He had pyorrhea and Louis Metcalf played the trumpet part. That was the first recording ever I made in my life.
If Louis Metcalf played the trumpet, what did King Oliver do?
No, King Oliver couldn't play, he had pyorrhea.
So, actually he didn't make the date.
It was King Oliver's date. It was in his name but he didn't play. Louis Metcalf played.
You mean Metcalf like ghosted for him and said this was King Oliver or did they give Louis Metcalf credit on the record?
Louis Metcalf made it on the record.
But did they give him credit for it, or did they say that was King Oliver?
No, they said it was King Oliver.
Oh, really?
Yeah. I've got the record with me.
I have to listen to that.

I'll have to do a whole lot of looking so you let me know by tomorrow. I don't listen to records. My wife she go in the back, and does. ... Sometimes 3 and 4 and 5 o'clock I hear music, pick there clappin her hands and well, she ... playing when the Saints Come Marching In, that's what she's listening to. And, I have quite a collection but I loan them out to people -- stupid. They break them. They Typical either say they forgot to bring them back. They story.
You're talking to someone who does that all the time. Donald Byrd.
(too many talking at once)
When you were younger and you were playing say at Morris Brown, could you name some of the other musicians that surrounded you in some of those early bands?
No one played in the band while I was there that never turned out professionally. Not one.
You were the only one?
I'm the only one.
You were 14 years old when you went in there?
Yeah, something like that.
When you first started to play?
Yeah.
What were the first things that you happened to learn how to play?
I don't know. I just started blowing.
Just blowing?

Blowing. I remember one night we had a white teacher and I still couldn't read but he would write on the board what he would want the trombone parts, you know, different parts to play. So, the first tune was Tuck Me to Sleep in My Old Kentucky Home. I remember the first eight bars after this many and that's as far as I went (sings the eight bars) and that was the big show MM. I'm not kiddin'. (inaudible) he wouldn't let no trombone I kept take it out ... we had about four trombones and played Bugle call and let every boy I was a kid and didn't know take a group called Rag. Everybody that was a big my better, I'd just go ahead and do my best and leave the shot ... (inaudible) rest.
When you were with King Oliver, was that called the Dixie Syncopators then?
What was that, Kid Oliver?
No, King Oliver?
Well, I don't know. The only thing I know was the man was King Oliver.
You don't know the name or what they called the band, though?
They said he was the greatest, one of the greatest trumpet players but I don't know nothing else about him -- just King Oliver's band.
What about Bunk Johnson?
Bunk Johnson?
Right.

Well, he's a trumpet player. I played a couple of engagements with him. They sent for him to come to New York and play one gig at the Army Club there on 52nd Street. And I played one, no, we did a recording down in New Jersey; and he's playing behind a crate too loud, pushing him further too loud; ... drunk, back ... He was old. He was way up in his 70s when he passed.
But, you didn't know him earlier?
No, no, no. I don't think I've spoken to him over, I haven't had over two conversations with him in my life.
When was your first encounter with Louis Armstrong?
Louis Armstrong?
Right.
What about him?
When did you first meet him or work with him?
Uh, let's see, where did I first meet him? We were playing, I was playing with Luis Russell's band in Savoy.
Didn't you join Luis Russell's band after Pops was leading the band?

Yeah, that's when I joined the band after ... '37 we were playing in Savoy and Louis Armstrong came from Chicago, you know, like to sit in. OK, excuse me. So when he finished his date and Louis Armstrong closed the engagement in Savoy, we went down to Saratoga Club Montgomery (?) and Louis Armstrong played one night down there with the Broadcasters (?). (indub.) And, ... we were playing at ... and Louis came to New York to get his own band. He came back with Louis Armstrong's band and Lionel Hampton was getting a band together. We were playin' in the Apollo Theatre. And Lionel asked Joe Glycer (?) said, "Who do you want to play with." I're to join him, want to play with Louis." So, that ... I stayed with him, I think, about six years, something like that.
You mentioned before that you made your first recording with King Oliver's band.
Yeah.
Were there two trombones in that band?
No.
Just you?
That's right.
Who else was in that -- that was in 1928 you said?
Yeah, in 1928, first of 1929. Yeah, we had Paul Bar Marvin on drums and Afs Foster on bass and Luis Russell.
That was with King Oliver or that was with -- was that King Oliver's band?
Yeah, but he was using his band. It wasn't King Oliver's band but the recording date was in his name.
Oh, I see, it was more like he made the date, yeah.
He thought he would be able to play but he weren't able to play so that's when they hired Louis Metcalf to play. But I joined Luis Russell, I forget what year it was. We were playing in the ...
You know why I was asking about King Oliver because there was a trombonist with King Oliver that ...
Kid Ory Kid
No, after King Ory. Honore Dutrey?
I don't know. Oliver I know he had two one was Tricky Sam Tricky sounds and the other one was Jimmy Harrison.
Yeah.
Yeah, cause they're the only two trombones that I remember. Of course, Tricky Simons (2) didn't really feature him. He and Sonny Greer, they'd with "King Them Bells" records like that.
When did you start coming in contact with Sidney Bechet? Moshey (?)?
We were, Uh, let's see. I was back, this was down in Saratoga, Club, and he came from Chicago, too, and (Errol Finan (?)) sat in with us and then I started making records with you know-
Do you happen to remember what year that was?
I sure don't remember but I know it was a helluva record. I'll never forget that. Sy Oliver made the arrangements, yeah. I have them, too.
They always talk about your relationship with Little Albert, Red Allen, that you have been associated with-
I sent to him to come to New York.
Where was he? When you sent for him, where was he?
He was in New Orleans.
Do you remember what year?
1929 or 1930 'cause we were playin' because we had a show down there, the Lenox Saratoga Club on 87 Avenue.
On Lenox Avenue in New Orleans?
No ... in New York.
I was getting ready to say there was another Lenox Avenue. And, where did you first hear him, Henry Red Allen?
I didn't hear him in person. I heard his record.
He had made records at that time, the 30s? in 1930
Henry "Red" Allen ... (made) ... a whole lot of records.
Do you remember what label?
I don't know.
Who did he record them with?
Well, different guys -- sometime I'd make two and three different recordings in one day with different bands.
How much were you getting paid a recording? then, about?
I don't know.
Do you have any idea? Ten dollars? How many?
I got mine. Yeah, I got mine, all right. And then Fletcher Henderson ... was playin' with him ... boy, he had a band, too.
When did you join Fletcher Henderson's band?
I don't know. Switched around so many times. I have those records back there, too. In fact, I have the whole album and I haven't played one of the records out yet. I went down to John Hammond's ...
What album is that? Fletcher Henderson album,
... do you want to see it?
Study in Frustration?

I don't know. At one time he called me up and said he wanted to see me so while I was down there he gave me this album, a Fletcher Henderson album and they all are in only one piece in the box. I don't play them.
When did you first meet with Albert Nicholas?
He was with Luis Russel's band.
So that was back in the 30s or something like that?
Yeah, '29 or '30.
And you recorded King Porter's song with Fletcher ... Stomp,
Yeah with Fletcher Henderson.
And, was it the Sugarfoot Stomp, too?
I think I made that with Louis Armstrong. I don't know, but I made it with somebody.
Did you know, what is his name, Jabbo? Javeral (?)?
Jabbo Smith? Oh, boy. What a man.
What was your impression of Jabbo?
Great, yeah, he was great.
Did he make many recordings?
I didn't know him that long. No, I didn't. But, I knew him long enough. Let's see what was he playing. I think he was playing down out at Sheldon Johnson's (?) ... ( ??? )
Do you remember what year or around what time?
It was in the early days he was walking around like this.
Jabbo Javeral (?), did he, how did he compare with Louis Armstrong?
I don't know how to compare them. But, the only thing I know I just loved his playing. And he played jazz. And I mean real jazz.
Can you think of any other significant trumpet players or anyone I mean like Jabbo(?)?
Yeah, Ed Swayzee(?).
Ed Swayzee(?)
Yeah.
Where was he from?
He's from Arkansas. That's a little bit before your time. Someone was asking me about him not so long ago.
Who did he play? in?
He could play to ...
Did you all work together at, you and Ed Swayzee?
No, we did for a while, yeah.
With who? With what band?
They had a show. You know, like you travel and we'd play together.
Do you remember what the name of the show was or whose show handled, whose show was that that you traveled with?
Jules(Mc_________), that's before your time.

You influenced like most of the trombone players since your time, I mean you've been like one of the major influences in jazz, I said and you have influenced so many young trombone players, I mean trombone players since your playing. What are some of the trombone players that you've listened to that you also we impressed by their playing ... or even younger ones.

I'd be glad to say it, Trummy Young. Note for note. He came and told me, he said, "I'm going to steal every thing that I can from you." And I said, "Thank you." It made me work harder. I have a record I made back there over in Denmark and the guy, I have his picture there, he sent for me. He owned a chocolate factory over there and he was a very nice guy. So, the first night I got there, got off the plane and ate dinner and he walked downstairs and said he wanted me to listen to a record. He played "I'm Confessing." (that phrases) I said it I know it's the same notes but then (I played) it a lot, you know.
And so Trummy had taken...
Trummy played but well, I thought it was me plenty of times. And I mean it made me feel good. ( ... ) Makes me try to do better.
You're a very important person. Sam What about Tricky Simon?
I couldn't do nothing with him, but hire his plunger. He always used his plunger ... when he's playing with Duke (??). So we were playing with Luis Russell and
we were both on the stand Duke ... so we used to play tricks on each other then. So you couldn't do nothing with my big plunger and I hid it ... (?)
I gave it back to him.
Did you take his plunger before he walked in the door...
Yeah, he'd reach down (...) solo and no plunger there.
So, what did he do?
He didn't do nothing. He used his hands.
I'll bet he was going crazy trying to figure out what happened.
He sure was but he didn't get angry about it. I mean it's clean fun, doing that kind of thing.
What was your impression of Kid Ory?

Kid Ory? I haven't been around him so many times. The last time we played together was at the, Newport News. We had three trombone players. We had Jack Teagarden, Kid Ory and myself, we played together on the same stand.
In Virginia?
No, Newport, Newport.
Oh, Newport, Rhode Island.
The jazz festival, yeah. You know he passed a couple of weeks ago.
Yeah, I know. What was your impression of him as a trombonist?
No, I don't want to make no kind of remark one way or the other. No, I just know he was one of these old-time trombone players, not playing a whole lot of jazz notes, doin' the less slide.
When Kid Ory was playing with Jelly Roll Morton, had you heard him?
Who was that?
Kid Ory?
not enough... No, that ... I don't remember him. No, I don't.
Because I was wondering what kind of effect the various trombonists had on your style, you know, in the development of ....
I'm not saying it for meanness but so help me God I have never tried to copy from nobody, ( ? ) I don't give a damn, I'm just going to be right or wrong. a colored trombonist, nobody. .... don't want
What is your impression of Jack Teagarden? (no answer)
He's okay. ( ? )
How many times did you two work together? Just on occasion?

No, see when I first came to New York ( ? ) so, anyway ... I'm not afraid to play with nobody... we'd get to work in the morning and every morning here's Jack Teagarden about 4 o'clock after the place had closed, I caught him. O'Neil Old Dale Spencer came and got me out of bed ... ( ? ) Willie the Lion Smith nothing but the piano ... and he was playing in the Nest ( ? )

... like this and I kept him there until 8 o'clock in the morning. I said, 'You ain't going nowhere.' Played Tiger Rag in every key. Every time he'd start off, I said, 'No, you're not.' Then, you know, sometimes they have agents and that things and you don't know who's listening to you. So, he decided to get up a cavalcade for jazz and Jack, he got _______.
So, we played and we got; Jack could play, too. And, he's a helluva executioner but I never ... I never called that jazz music
(too much noise)
Yeah, right.
How about _______?
Every night he came to work, he drank and I drank. He had a special quart in a case, playing my horn. ... we were friends, we just played ... liked to have fun.

One of the things that I was very interested in was the time that you were playing with Luis Russell's band and with Louis Armstrong, when Pops was conducting, was in front of the band because like that seems like that was a very important time in your life. That was in the '30s?
Yeah
wasn't it? I know I read somewhere, matter of fact in this book you just gave me here I was reading it says that you played with Luis Russell from 1929 to 1931. Is that true?
Yes, it is true.
But, then you played with Luis Russell longer than that. You left the band in '31?

And played with Louis Armstrong. Went from Russell to Armstrong. Armstrong took over Luis Russell's band. He conducted the band until he got ready to fire Luis Russell and then he fired him (inaudible). So I stayed on with Louis until 1940. Then New Years we went down to Cafe Society with Red Allen downtown.

You've made a lot of records with the band, Pop's band at that time and I was listening to some of the things like I Double Dare You. You took a solo on that -- it's fantastic. As well as the things that you did like the band that Pops had where you recorded When The Saints Go Marching In.
But, I like By and By best.
Tell me, you said you made a statement about, that Jack Teagarden's playing wasn't jazz, what would you call it?
Execution.
Just execution?
That's right. That's the only way that I can explain it.
Where do you think he got his ...
Everything he played comes from the book, I'll put it like that. He just played the chords that they got cut the..
Very little feeling.
Of course, I don't know anything about chords. You tell me he played this chord or that chord, I don't know. ( ? ) You put your hand there,, ( ? ) ... (some interference)
But you just play it from your ear, whatever you heard?
No, I ... I've been collecting royalties since 1929. I wrote how many tunes?
How many tunes have you written?
I don't really -- got to check them out. But, I've been collecting twice a year since 1929.
From where? From where? From Where?
From Higginbotham Blues, Give Me Your Telephone Number and a guy will call me up and say ... and there's some other tunes. I don't know. played the record the other day swing out,
You don't know how many tunes you've written.
I sure don't. I know how many I wrote, four?
Four tunes?
Where is the money coming from?
Oh, it comes from the royalty companies. They have to send me the money.
What publishing company?
I don't know. ( ? ) I think ... Higginbotham Blues is on an OKeh record. I'm sure of that because it was 9 o'clock in the morning
But you don't know like (..?)
What they did after that, you see the government took over.
Oket records?

On all the records. You write a tune, you're going to get paid for it today. Once upon a time, you know, its like, I'm with a band and I think up a tune and I tell the leader, And the leader says to me, "Well, if you let me put my name on that, so and so and so and so, I will record it for you." And that's the way you did it. They'll get it to you.
Did Luis Russell, did he do things like that?
No.
Louis Armstrong?
No, he wasn't like that.
What about Louis Armstrong?
No.
What about Fletcher Henderson?
I don't remember. No.
But that was a common practice at that time like you and write a tune, what about even playing it on a bandstand?
Well, they don't ask for nothing.
Well, the band leaders would let you play that tune on the bandstand, I mean if he liked it or something?
well, he's gonna play it, ... I mean if the leader said, "Play it," the leader made the arrangement. He said, "We're going to play this."
So you didn't make the arrangements on your tunes or anything?
No, I didn't make arrangements.
On your tunes, on your Blues and so forth, who gets the credit for that?
I do, cause I'm on it.
Does anybody else ...

... over and over and over again until the guy listens and you put it down and that's the way we get 'em like that. I have a tune now I wrote when I was in the hospital. It's a good one, too. You better do your thinking before you start your drinking, ... I got the lyrics to it; nobody knows about it but me.
You got to give it to Donald or myself and maybe we can record it ourselves or get someone to record it for you.
Maybe. We'll see about it.
Okeh On your OK recordings, who recorded that the blues (?)? ...
Mostly Luis Russell's band.
Most of the composition was done by Luis Russell's band?
Yeah.
And you get all of the credit, 100 percent of the credit?
I get what?
All of the credit, nobody else gets credit?
No, no, no. Nobody gets credit but me. Just my name (?) written by J. C. Higginbotham. Everybody get paid.
Did you ever write any songs that came out under somebody else's name?
No. Louis and me have got one, I got a guy that's (?) I never had ... Everything is still OK.
Everything is still OK?
Yes. It's the only way we could record it was with Millinder's Lucky Middleton's (?) band.
What year was that?
About 1930 something ... That's when we wrote Ride, Red, Ride.
Ride, Red, Ride?
Yeah.
That was Henry 'Red' Allen?

... He never would let nobody play. Red Allen could play ... he and Lucky Miller (?), Attlee. Of course, you never heard no trombone player play jazz. You hear trumpets now But you never heard no trombones.

Yeah, well, that's why we were talking about the Luis Russell period because like I know he recorded a lot of songs and I didn't know some of the songs were your songs. I know there was a period when you came with the band, with Luis Russell's band or with Louis Armstrong's band, you were with Luis Russell's band and then Louis Armstrong came in front of the band.
That's right.
Well, what I wanted to ask you about was some of the musicians that were in that band when some of those things were recorded like West End Blues, you mentioned By and By.
You know the West End Blues?
(Sings opening of West End Blues)
Everything happening ... (comment inaudible)
That's the way I practice at home -- good exercise.
How's that, the doo, da, doo, la, loo?
Oh, yeah. When you get to (.?)
Because I have West End Blues here, have you heard it lately?
... (inaudible) (plays the record) (comments during the record inaudible but refer to JCH's solo) ...
Red Allen, Otis Johnson ...
(Sing w. Armstrong solo)
That's Louis Armstrong's trumpet, Red Allen back there.
Luis Russell's band.
And the solo you take on this is fantastic. You remember that solo?
After I first started (?)
(During guitar solo) who's that?
Luis Russell.
Playing guitar?! Piano?
How did the people do for this when y'all played this in person?
Loved it. (??)
Who were some of the other members in the band?
Greely Walton, Charley Holmes...
Charley Holmes the saxophonist
Albert Nicholas. Red Allen, Ctis Johnson, (?) trumpets. (?)
How about, wasn't Wilbur DeParis in that band with you?
Not, that was Louis Armstrong's band.
Well, when this was recorded, this was with just one trombone?

Yeah.
(END OF RECORD)
That's interesting because I thought Wilbur DeParis was in that band along with you. I mean like when you recorded West End Blues and By and By.
When the Saints Come Marching In, that was just one trombone?
Big band.
Oh, that was the big band?
Yeah. Maybe Wilbur was in it.
Yeah, I think so because I/some of those records ...
I'm not sure.
And George Washington?
Yeah, he was in that. He was in Lucky Millinder's band.
But, didn't he work with you in Luis Russell's band or Louis Armstrong's band?
No, he worked in Lucky Millinder's band. funny guy.
He was funny.
Funny and how.
How? He used to keep everybody laughing in the band.
Clowning and carrying on.
Clowning while he was playing?
Yeah. He didn't care what he did.
What did he do, what kind of things? Do you remember some of the things he used to do? What kind of things would he do?
Oh, he'd get up and shake his self and he had some kind of (2) hit him across the head. But, he was lots of fun.
You all did a lot of traveling with that band?
And how.
How did you all travel?
By bus, yeah. And we got through the Holland Tunnel ... he got out the bus and kissed the ground. He had been traveling so much.
How long would you all, you know when you would leave New York, about how long would you all stay out on the road?
I don't know. We went out I think for more than a year ... with Lucky's band.
What was your impression of people like Paul Whiteman and Benny Goodman?
Bill Davis?
No, Paul Whiteman, and Benny Goodman.
I think he's very nice.
... Yeah, I met him. I remember meeting him a couple of times. That was when we were playing across from him at Roseland. We had Bill Polk (?).
Do you remember what year that was?

But I mean not at that particular time?
No, I didn't know anything about him then.
You played with the bands at the Eighty-One and Ninety-One, right?
Beg pardon?
You played there?
Yes, he played there.
Would you describe what the band was like and some of the people that may have been in the band?
I didn't know anything about Frank Johnson until I came to New York and they sent for him to come -
He said the band that was playing at Eighty-One. Do you remember any of the people that were in it?
No.
And then you left, after playing at the Eighty-One and the rooftop and around Atlanta, you left and then came to Cincinnati?
Yes.
And in Cincinnati, what did you do?
He went back to school, tailoring school.
What school was that? Do you remember? The name of the school in Cincinnati?
Oh, that was the Clothing Industrial School. That's the name of it... (SEVERAL VOICES) Yeah, that's when I was taken care of.
Stella - another sister - she went there too. She was going to _____ also.
How long did he remain in the school there?
Beg pardon?
How long did you stay in the school in Cincinnati?
Mm, off and on, let's see, I went and I came back - the last time I stayed there about - I left in 1927 and I stayed there about a year, because I was playing with Wes Helvey's band.
Did you - did they have a school band at the Industrial School?
School band?
Yes.
At the school?
Right.
No, no, no... I just took tailoring there. I was taking tailoring at night, going to night school.
What did you do during the day?
I worked for the Jenning (illegible) Motor Company.
How did you meet Wes Helvey?
I went to visit my sister and Clarence Page who lived next door, he had a band and he heard me practice. So he told Wes Helvey about me.
What did he play?
He played sax, tenor sax. He had his own band.
Clarence Page?
Clarence Page, yeah.
And he introduced you to Wes Helvey?
Yeah.
Who was in that band with Wes Helvey?
Uh-oh, let's see, we got a fellow work here now. He works here where Samuel works, on the elevator - Henry Jameson.
He works where.
He works on the elevator there.
Where?
Right here where Sandy Williams works, on - what street is that ninety something Street; and Edgan Courance, tenor sax player -
Where did you play with Wes Helvey?
I played in Cincinnati.
But I mean where?
We played all over... That's where I met my wife, down in Charleston. We played down in Charleston, that's where I met her.
Oh, so you used to travel?
Yeah, we did lots of traveling.
Did you encounter any other people, day other bands and things like that during your traveling? Did you meet other musicians out of other bands?
Oh, yeah, sure.
Who were some of the people that you met at that time?
... We played out in Dallas and I met Alphonse (Adolphus?) Trent's band. He had one of the best bands in Dallas.
What was his name?
Adolphus Trent. Stuff Smith was playing with him then.
Do you remember what year this was?
I got a bad memory.
You worked with Wes Helvey's band from 1924, you said, until about when? How long?
I worked with him until 1927 when they sent for me to come here.
You came to Cleveland in 1926, that you forgot, because you played down at the Globe Theatre.
When you left Helvey's band, who did you go with then?
They sent for me to come to Buffalo and I went to work with Eugene Primos' band. He had a band there. Then I left his band and worked with Jimmy Harrison's band.
The first band that you were in, in Buffalo, do you remember what year it was and who was in it?
And who was in the band?

Myself, trombone player; Eugene Primos, drums; and called him 'Jesse' Wilson. Ralph Wilson, violinist, one of the best... Let's see who else. Percy - I think it's Percy Sutton, piano player. I'm not sure, I know his first name was Percy.
And how long did you stay with that band?
Oh, about a year.
Where did you travel with that band?

Oh, we played on a steady job there. So we went out up here in New York - Albany - to play a gig and that was in September. So I said, I'm so close to my mother I'll go and pay a visit. September 1928 and at 8 o'clock I had two jobs...

How do you think you got those jobs? Were people talking about Jay C. Higginbotham, the trombone player? Were people, other musicians, talking about Jay C. Higginbotham, the trombonist, so when you came to New York to see your mother - everybody was interested in hearing you?
Yeah. Willie Lynch and Chick Webb both knew me and had heard of me. They both tried to hire me.
Willie Lynch?
Yeah.
Where were they?
They were in the Savoy.
So they both wanted you to work with that band?
Yeah. The bass player heard me and he went out and got Louis Russell and told him about me. So Russell asked me to work for him and that's when I started playing with Louis Russell.
At that particular time you say you didn't work with Willie Lynch or Chick Webb?
No, but I worked with Chick Webb later.
After that. That's 1928 and you say you worked with
- you started to work with Louis Russell's band. You talked about some of the people who were in Louis Russell's band.
How long did you stay with that band?
Louis Russell's?
Right.
Oh, I don't know.
I know you were with him in '29 because I came to see you in Saratoga, the Saratoga Club.

When you were with Louis Russell's band you made a record that you let me hold the other day - 1929, 1930, Louis Russell - 'Jersey Lightning.' Do you remember some of those songs - Jersey Lightning, Feeling the Spirit, Doctor Blues, 'New' Call of the Freaks? Tell us something about it.
I don't know nothing to tell you...

There were a lot of musicians who were on those records. Can you recall when you recorded those records? When you were in the studio with Louis Russell's band it must have been a big thing for you. Wasn't this one of the first recordings that you had made?

The first recording I made was with Louis Russell's band but it was supposed to have been King Oliver's band. But King Oliver couldn't play and Louis Metcalf played. That was the first record I made with Louis Russell.
What was the name of that song?
I don't remember it.
One that you made?
His very first record.
That wasn't Your Telephone Number, was it?
I don't remember, sweetheart.
I have also asked - you really have to think about this - when you recorded those records with Louis Russell, you remember how much money musicians were getting paid?
We were getting the scale, whatever it was.

I think around $50.
$50, that much?
Something like that.

We would do four sides.
How long would it take you to record one?
The time on the record was about 3 minutes and 15 seconds.
Did you go over the songs many times?
I don't know how many times. Of course, see, we knew practically all the tunes ... because we were playing on a steady job and we used to play them practically every night.
So you would get $50 for recording four songs?
Yeah.
A lot of those songs were written by Louis Russell and -
Yeah. Call of the Freaks - who wrote Jersey Lightning - Louis Russell.
The drummer who played with you? What was his name?
Paul.
Do you remember the drummer who played with you?
Paul Barbavin
He wrote some songs also.
Oh yeah, he wrote a lot of them.
How about when Louis Russell and Paul wrote these songs, did they get paid for writing the songs?
Sometimes.

On one of the records Louis Metcalf played trumpet, you on trombone, Albert Nicholas, Teddy Hill played tenor saxophone, Will Johnson guitar, Moore bass, Fats Picon ... /When Jay C. To EK: came to New York in 1928, did you follow his career?
Yes.
Because working with Louis Russell's band, that was a pretty famous band, so it was pretty nice to have a brother who was working with a famous band like that.
I came over here during that time. He was playing at the Saratoga Club, downstairs, and I came over here.

I know he was a busy little fellow, I can tell you that! ... with the older boys.
(NOISE ON TAPE)

Quite often. (LAUGHTER)

He was busy all the time.

To the farm?
Yes.

Oh, he was too small.

..... He had people working with him. There was 3 other houses on the plantation and they were sharecroppers. My father furnished everything and what they made, they gave him half.

I really don't know. in the grove and the other houses set on the side.
Seems like a lot of property for a black man to own at that time. That's why I asked how -
Yes, it was about the biggest farm down there.
Can you describe anything about your father and mother?
parents, that's all I know.

No, my grandmother, I know she was half Indian on my father's side.
What about the other?

What was he like?
He was a nice old gentleman. He was part Indian too.
Did you see your other grandpa?
No. (NOT CLEAR - BABY IS CRYING)

No, only my grandmother on my father's side.
... I'd like to get some idea of what it was like musically in Cincinnati when you were playing. Were there a lot of clubs? Were there a lot of jazz bands?
Yeah. Sure was.
...What kind of music were they playing there jazz music. Did it have the Midwestern-Chicago type of sound or did it have -
I don't know about Chicago. People talk about New Orleans style and different ones. The only thing I know they just played jazz music.
No, I mean the kind of sound that we get, the boogie-woogie -
No, no, they played just like they're playing now.
Like in New York?
Yeah, that's the way they played then, like we played around about Fletcher Henderson's days.
It was all Dixieland?
Yeah, they played it.
In Atlanta also?
Yes, I would say - mostly ragtime music before Dixieland...
We didn't play no Dixieland. The first time I played Dixieland was down in Bridgeport. Red Allen was playing there and I joined his band from Boston. ... You know when I was in Cleveland?
Yes. But when you came to New York, that was Dixieland music, wasn't it?
That wasn't no Dixieland. That was straight jazz because I didn't know Dixieland music. Red Allen played mostly Dixieland music.
How would you describe, in your words, the difference between the Dixieland music and the ragtime?
That's just about impossible.
I mean, if you played in a ragtime band, how would -
They mostly used trombones for slide, you know.
For ragtime?
Dixieland and ragtime, yeah.
What were the other instruments playing? Who was playing the melody line?
Who was playing the melody? On these tunes? Red Allen.
No, in a Dixieland orchestration, the makeup of the band.
The trumpet player usually played. ... (SINGS)...

It doesn't take long because even now I could bring a tune out here if I had my chops and play any kind of tune I ever heard. All you have to do is fill in, listen, and fill in in the right time and right place. Dixieland tunes, they have special notes, but Red would teach me, you know, during intermission, take me upstairs and tell me. You say before that you were playing jazz?
Real jazz music, yeah.
What were the other instruments, like you said the trumpet player played the lead and the trombone played their part. What was the clarinet and the saxophone and the others doing?
Say it again.
What other - what melodic lines did the other instruments play?
I don't know - they were playing their own stuff. They know how to keep off each other. When you know a tune, you know
how to keep off each other. It's like three of you would start singing a tune now and if all three of you knew it, you knew what part to sing. Like that.
They would know the harmonic part to play?
No, just keep off each other.

Now, we're into the 1930's, with the time that you were playing with Louis Russell, 1928 to 1930 you said you played with him. Who did you play with after that, right after you left Louis Russell's band?
I played with Louis Armstrong.
What year was that?
See, that was Louis Russell's band.
What year was this?
I don't know what year it was ... Lionel Hampton and Louis Russell. we was in a theatre.
What happened in 1931?
You were with Fletcher Henderson before you went together.
Who was in that band at the time?
Fletcher Henderson's band? 1931 was this?
Oh brother! We had Sandy Williams, (Y.) Williams, (Y) Jay C. Higginbotham, (Y.) Bobby Stark, (Y.) Coleman Hawkins - everybody in the band was (Y.)
Was Don Redman there?
Yes, Don Redman. And Rex Stewart was with us for a while and Bob Stark and Billie Holiday's father, Clarence Holiday.
Played guitar?
Yeah, and John Kirby and Russell Smith.
How long did you stay with Fletcher Henderson?
I don't know.
Was that '31, '32, two years, three years?
Two or three years, something like that.
When you left him you went with -
She knows better than I do.
That's when you went with Louis, because I was keeping up with them because they were usually playing Cleveland at least once in that time.
So he traveled with that band for a while?
Yes.
Did he do any recordings with the band as a whole?
With Fletcher? I've got the whole album of that. John Hammond gave it to me, the whole album.
So then you went from there to Louis Armstrong, or back with Louis Russell?
Lou Russell and from Lou Russell - it was still Russell's band but Louis Armstrong took over.
You say you played with Fletcher Henderson for about 4 years?
Three or four years, something like that.
What kind of things did you -
Encounter in that time?
What did you get involved in, in that time? What was it like with the band?
With Fletcher?
Right.
Nothing but plain fun. We didn't do nothing but have a ball.
Can you describe some things that you did?
One thing, he was just a and he'd let you do like you want. He'd say he wanted you there at 8 o'clock. You'd get there about 9. Coleman Hawkins was a great one on that one. Nobody made time, nobody.
And he didn't make time because he called at my house.
Did that have an effect on the band working?

If Fletcher wanted you to start playing at 9 o'clock, he'll tell you about 7:30 or 8. Coleman Hawkins was always the leader on that one. He'd come in around about an hour late and then follow the leader, and we got used to it. If you didn't drink you weren't a member of the band.
You weren't a member of the band if you didn't drink?
You weren't a member of the band.
Is that when you started to drink?
Everybody in the band drank.
Did you start to drink at that time with Fletcher?
No, I drank before.
Fletcher didn't drink, did he?
Fletcher? Oh, brother! Yes sir, but you never see him
high when he's directing. He drank afterward.
You mentioned Coleman Hawkins was in that band with you and Fletcher and Charles Holiday.
Clarence.
Clarence Holiday. Could you just fill us in on what kind of things did the musicians, each of them - did you ever hear Coleman Hawkins practicing during those times that you were with -
I never heard him practice in my life.
Did you practice?
None.
You never played your instrument in the daytime?
Very seldom, just pick it up -
But you had jam sessions -
Get on the job and play about a half hour - because we knew the tunes of some of the music we had to read. We had the music all the time.
But I mean, did you feel content, did you feel that you were improving on your instrument?
I was very content with everybody.
Where were you working. You were working like one-nighters? All across the country?
Every place.
Did you go out to California?
We had a private bus, you know.
How did you all get paid? Did you get paid by the week?
Yeah.
So you were on salary for a week? Suppose you worked one day in that week, did you get paid still?
No.
How would you get paid if you worked one day?
You didn't get paid.
You got paid for that one day.

Yeah. ... When we'd leave New York Fletcher's agent would have all these routines made out where we were going to play. We would make a copy so we would know where to write our chicks telling them what time to meet us...
There are some other things about the Fletcher Henderson band that I would like to know about. I had asked about the practicing; you say you never heard any of the musicians really practicing.
We would rehearse sometimes....
Did you all jam together and play music other than the music you were playing with Fletcher Henderson?
Yes, oh yes.
Was Fletcher Henderson playing like that?
Oh sure.
Would Fletcher Henderson play a song like 'Body and Soul'?

He featured it with somebody in the band - he featured it with a guy in the band. You know, just like any other band, if you had a solo you wanted to play, then you know, call on him, he'd go ahead and do it.

While you were with Fletcher's band you recorded some records with him. Do you remember some of the people who were in charge of recording records at that time? You mentioned John Hammond was there? Did you only record for John Hammond or were there other people who were responsible for putting together musicians to make a record?
No, I don't.
John Hammond was the only one?

Someone else - I can't think of his name. This was up in Boston. Stribling Brothers. They did all the booking up in Boston. Booked all the bands up there, Stribling Brothers, 'cause if we'd go up there, you know, we wouldn't go for a night or something like that. We'd make a tour through New England.

Going on after Fletcher Henderson's band, you went with Louis Russell and Louis Armstrong was heading the band. How long did you work with that band? And what year did you start working with that band?
I forget what year it was but I know what year I quit.
What year did you quit?
1940, New Year's, I joined Red Allen's band, Cafe Society.
Right. Do you know approximately when you left Fletcher Henderson's band?
... You left Lou Armstrong and went with Red Allen. I know he was with Lou Armstrong in 1936. Then I came to Cleveland in 1938 and you were still with Lou Armstrong. I mean I came to New York.
Could you approximate when he left Fletcher Henderson?
He left Fletcher Henderson about 19 -
I didn't quit the band because I didn't like Lou. I just got tired of traveling.
Why did you leave Fletcher Henderson?
I was curious and I just liked to keep going.
He left Fletcher Henderson about 1932 or 3. About 1932 I believe.
Something like that.
That means you played with Fletcher Henderson's band for about two years?
Something like that.
But you say you joined Fletcher Henderson's band in 1930, after you had left Louis Russell? Is that correct?
I think that's correct because they played here in Cleveland in 1930 - in 1930 they played Cleveland.
I know when we came to Cleveland because that's when ...
(NOT CLEAR)
Could you explain anything about that time up until - what songs you recorded and anything about Louis Armstrong at that period?
Explain anything?
Yes. What you recorded, what the band was like, what was Louis Armstrong like.
The greatest in the world! Greatest, and he'd always see

that I played something, always, because he and I were like this. He would sit here and I would sit here, and Lou and I were like this. We'd get the work, we'd go out, you know, to do one-nighters. He'd say, "Come on now, let's go out and sport a while." We were like that. I didn't even give him two-weeks notice because I was ashamed. I gave it to the manager.
Who was the manager?
Joe Garland.
He was the manager of the band? Not Joe Glaser?
Joe Garland.
The arranger.
So, why did I leave. It took me two days, three days. They wouldn't let me get on a plane.
When you were working with Louis Armstrong did you have any contact with the people who were taking care of Louis Armstrong's business, like Joe Glaser?
Oh, he had his own valet and sometimes Joe Glaser would travel with us, just ride around for fun...
When you first joined Louis Armstrong's band, about how much money a week were you making?
A hundred and some dollars.
About $120?
More than you usually got in a band. Fifty dollars a night.
How much?
Fifteen dollars a night and the other guy got $10 a night.
He would pay musicians different things because different people were more important.
That's exactly right. The trombone player he got $10 and I got $15 and when he gave it to me, he got mad. That was George Washington.
If you work every night, seven nights, did you all do that quite often - work seven nights a week, seven different one-nighters?
Yeah, we did mostly one-nighters then.
Your sister said that you were featured on certain numbers like I'll Be Glad When You're Dead You Rascal You, Saints Go Marching In, Bye and Bye.
'Saint James Infirmary.' Were you featured on that?
Yeah, I was.
Is there anything that stands out in your mind about that particular period of time?

A particular tune I feature now. This is one that Louis made and he featured me on that tune, but when I get my own band I was feature myself on it. I just like it because I made it tough. I'm not bragging on myself, you know, but made it tough for other guys to play.
Then you said you left and you joined Henry Red Allen?
Yeah.
How did that come about?
John Hammond sent for me. Red had John Hammond to send for me in Memphis, Tennessee.
You were in Memphis, Tennessee, with Louis Armstrong?
That's where I took a plane from.
To California to meet Red Allen?
No, from Memphis to New York.
What did John Hammond have to do with Red Allen?
He had something to do with practically all the musicians.
How?
Well, he had the money. He'd book you and he'd get recordings for you. He's doing the same thing now.
You and Red had been friends, though, in the band with Louis Armstrong, right?
I sent for Red Allen to come here.
When?
What were the circumstances? Why did you send for him?
I don't know. I just, you know, like I hear people talk about I'd never heard him and I'd never seen him play. We were playing the Saratoga Club.
This was with Louis Russell?

Louis Russell's band and we had - what was the trumpet player, man from New Orleans, and he couldn't read, so I wrote Red a letter and told Louis Russell that I was ready for Red, so he sent for him. That's when Red came here.
So the trumpet player who couldn't read?
What's his name? But he could play. I can't think of his name.
What did you all have to read?
We had arrangements too, you know.
Arrangements that Louis Russell wrote?
Yeah. But he couldn't read at all. So we had to let him go, he couldn't keep up with the band.
Where did you learn how to read then?
I taught myself, 15 cents.
But you said that you sent for him and then you and Henry Red stayed very close associates, right?
Yeah. He quit, I quit; I quit, he quit. He went with Mills' Blue Rhythm Band, he sent for me and I quit.
What band was that?

Mills' Blue Rhythm Band. When I was with Lucky's band we were in Philadelphia and I got a telegram from Fletcher Henderson, asking me to call him. I've got it in the scrapbook. He said, "I want to talk to you about Red Allen." That's when Red and I went with Fletcher. We'd switch around like that.
So this was during the 30's that you were switching around in the bands?

It's just like holding a conversation. You understand each other when you talk. I knew what Red was going to play anytime and he knew what I was going to play, so we understood each other by playing. But other than that, that was about it.
Tell me, while you were working with Louis Armstrong's band, Red Allen was in that band with you. Did Red Allen get much
Yeah, during intermission. We would take intermissions and then Red would play 30 minutes with the band while we were resting.
How did the people -
Respond?
Respond to Red Allen's playing?
Very good.
The same way they responded to Louis Armstrong's playing?
Yes, very good. You might as well get things straight, very good.
How did Red Allen look on Louis Armstrong? I mean, did Red Allen ever look at him and say, "Wow, he can really play! He can do things that I can't do."
I don't know how to explain that. Red's got a funny disposition so I can't explain that.
How long were you with Lucky Millinder's band and when was that period? (To EK: Do you remember when he was with Lucky Millinder?)
He wasn't with him too long, were you?
No, not that long.
That was during the 30's?
Yes, all during the 30's.
When he left he was with Fletcher Henderson, then Lucky Millinder? You said John Hammond was doing all the recording of
all of the bands and so forth. That was with Columbia Records?
That's right...(?)
So how did John Hammond - I guess he got to Red Allen and got to know you and Red Allen from your playing during the 30's, and then did he form the band for Red?

He talked Red into hiring me. When you got money, you can do a lot of things. He told Red, "Why don't you send for Higgy?" So Red said O.K. John Hammond sent me a plane ticket and $50. It took me 3 days to get on there. They didn't want no negros on the plane. So John Hammond said, "You don't put him on there we're going to sue you."
Where did you join Red Allen?
Cafe Society Downtown, New Year's.
New Year's, what year?
New Year's, 1940.
And how long did you stay there?
Oh, I don't know how long we stayed down there. We stayed down there till they fired us. He told Red Allen if he didn't get rid of somebody he was going to fire the whole band.
I came here in '45 and you and Red were playing at the Onyx Club.
Yeah, we went from Downtown up to the Onyx Club.
So in other words, from '40 to almost '45 he was at the Cafe Society?
Yeah, we left Cafe Society and went to 52nd Street.
Did you work with anyone else between '40 and '45 beside Red?
No.
Where did you travel at the time?
No, we just played here in New York on 52nd Street. We played Kelly's Stable, we played the Three Deuces, and we played the Onyx Club, all on the same street.
How big was the band?
We had 6 pieces.
Who was in the band?
We had Billy Taylor on bass.
Is that Billy Taylor's father?
I don't know about the son. He was a bass player, a good one, Hodgkins. They had Kenny Kersey on piano and Jimmy on drums, Edmund Hall on clarinet.
And that was it, you were ready. And did that band stay together a long time like that or did other people come in and out of the band? Did that band remain the same?
It remained the same.
From 1940 to 1945 while you were working -
Something like that. Didn't nobody get fired. I don't remember nobody getting fired.
How much were you making a week with that band when you went to Cafe Society?
Did you continue to make $200 the whole time that you worked with that band?
It's according to where you play.
What kind of things were you doing with that money? That was a lot of money at that time, in 1940, $200 a week.
Spending it.
I know, but on what? What kind of things would you buy? You had the best clothes of all the musicians around.
Just went out and had a good time.
And giving it away also.
Giving it away, helping other people. I had a whole lot of people to help.
How do you mean? Your family?
Relatives.
Your sister said that she saw you in Chicago and you said that you were out in California too?
He was in California in '45.
I went out there twice.
And again in '46 he was in Chicago because I went to Chicago to see him.
I'm sure glad she did.
But they had different musicians by that time, because there was Mole /the drummer - what was his name? I know you called him Mole - the drummer? Burne (Burns)
His name was Eddie Burns and we called him the Mole.
And you had Don Stovall.
What was Eddie's last name? Bourne
Burns.
Did the band change in 1945, start changing? What happened from '45 to '50?

... I know we went back to California again. We played out there twice. We played the Savoy first time, it was downtown, and we went back again and we played downtown. I forget the name of that place. We played three places. We played the Club 81. That was on Wilshire Boulevard, go straight out the Boulevard and it was right on the corner, Club 81.
Did you do any recordings in that period of time?
No, not out there.
What about from '40 to '45? Do you do much recording? With Red Allen and the band?
Yeah, but I don't remember how many recordings we made, so many.
Were many of those recordings for John Hammond?
Well, not all of them.
Who else did you record for during that period?
Oh, brother, let's see. Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw, Coleman Hawkins, Teddy Wilson, the All-Star Band?
What was the All-Star Band?
That was when they were supposed to be picking all the best musicians.
Was that Esquire?
I think so. ... 'One-O'clock Jump.'
Metronome?
Esquire. Esquire magazine used to run a poll - I think they started about 1935 or something like that, didn't they?
I don't know. This guy used to have it every day.
I remember '37.
How many polls did you win? How often?
I won more than anybody. Red told me I did; I don't know.
About eleven.
Yeah.
Did you win the first one?
Yeah.
About 1935.
I won the second through all of them. Bill Harris won one. I won eleven.
So you won just about until they stopped making the poll, I think about 1950 or something like that. Tell me something -
The first one, I got a picture of it somewhere. My sister's got one. I lost them in storage. They were so beautiful it broke my heart.
When you were winning all these polls, that was kind of telling, not only the world, but the older musicians, the other musicians, that you were one of the best trombonists around.
You know, there was no other trombonist that was really comparing to you because you were winning all the polls.
I wasn't trying to win; I was just playing.
How did the other trombonists feel about you, the other trombonists who were around playing at that time?
What? I don't know how they felt -
I mean, how did they treat you like - you know you were really the greatest trombonist.
We made these recordings. People sent in votes for you and whoever gets the most votes wins.
They still have that. What I want to find out is -

(END OF TAPE) ?
No

INTERVIEW WITH JAY C. HIGGINBOTHAM
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION - HISTORY OF JAZZ
The other trombonists, like - you take a trombonist, O.K., Tricky Sam.
Tricky never won.
I know he never won but, you were always winning, so how did he feel about you? Did he feel that he could cut you when he played?
I don't think so; I don't think nobody felt like that. Nobody felt like that, nobody.
Did you have a lot of trombonists who would say, "Come on, come on to this jam session. I can play better than you."
Yeah, there was one guy who would do that.
Who was that?

What's his name? He's dead now. George Stevens - I don't think you know him. George Stevens. Oh yeah, another one, he's living now but he's not playing. He wrote me a letter. He's with Zack Whyte's band in Cincinnati and he was coming to New York. His name was Stumpy Brady. You know him.
Stumpy, yes.

He wrote me a letter. He said, I'm going to come to New York and teach you how to play. So we met in the Savoy after we got through and went to the Rhythm Club. So I wasn't showing off, just took out the horn and started playing ... There wasn't nobody there playing but him. They left him in there by himself.

Was that the time when came T6 over and played with you? ... He was playing the Brass Rail T7 in Chicago and when he and Red finished there they came to Cleveland. He and Red came to Cleveland and Red went on to New York and Jay stayed there with me.
How long did he stay?
He stayed there about two months.
Yeah, something like that.
I don't think Red was working here then, they weren't doing anything here then, so he played there at the Tijuana Club.
What year was this, again?
It was 1950.
So then from 1945 until 1950 what did you do?
I don't know ... (JCH and HIS SISTER BOTH TALK HERE.)
You played in Boston...
Where did he work in Boston?
I worked in the Savoy and I worked in the High-Hat. I had Rex Stewart in my band out there.
Oh, you had a band?
Yes, I had two bands.
Then you weren't working with Red between '45 and '50?
I had Rex Stewart in my first band. stop
When did you start that band?
That was after the 50's. That was about '53.
So in other words, you stayed with Red up until '50?
About 10 years.
About 10 years you and Red - the whole 40's you stayed with Henry Red Allen? Is that correct?
I don't know. But I know how long I stayed in Boston. I went to New York from Boston.
That was about '50. That was about '52.
And opened in Wally's first, Wally's Paradise and then I went to the Savoy...
While you were playing with Red, or while you were all playing around, I'm sure you must have bumped into musicians like Charlie Parker.
Never met Charlie Parker in my life.
How about Dizzy Gillespie?
Oh, yeah,he and I were buddies.
How about all the musicians who were around Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, like the pianist Thelonious Monk? How did you feel about the music they were playing?

In the beginning I didn't like Dizzy's playing because he spoiled a whole lot of musicians. That's when this Juilliard thing started, you know, he'd put on his beret and go around with his horn and everyone wanted to do a Dizzy... I told him, "You're spoiling the other musicians. You're too great for that. You can play different." So he changed and then he went back again. He could play any style he wanted.
What did you think of Jazz Johnson?
I never did know what to think of him. I can't understand nothing but a whole lot of notes.
When did you first meet Jay Jay?
We were playing in the Red Allen band. We were playing at the Three Deuces and he had three pieces there during intermission.
What year was this?
I was kidding with him. He stayed mad with me all the time but I was kidding with him, you know.
About what year was that?
He was a heck of a musician, but I can't understand - he didn't play jazz music, not in my opinion, nothing but ... execution, that's the only thing I could hear.
Did you ever work with Duke Ellington at any time?
Yeah, I made a recording. I made a date with him in Philadelphia, spent a weekend there working. Then I made a recording with him in New York.
When was this? In the 40's, 30's?

Had to be in the 30's because we were in the studio and that's when they were having these all-star records. Bill Harris was on one side and I was on the other side. Sy Oliver made an arrangement and Duke made one side. Sy wouldn't give him no solo. Duke said, 'Uh-huh...' That's when we made the first side.
What was the name of it?
He was sitting at the piano and he did like this. I said, 'What is that for?' He said, 'You just play anything you want as long as you get ready. This is your introduction.' And that's what I did.
What was the name of the song?
I don't know.
You (had) that record?
I broke it.
You don't remember the name of the song? You don't remember the year? Could you tell me about when you recorded with Jelly Roll Morton?
No, I can't. I got the record back there but I don't remember it.
Did you work with him for any period of time?
No, just recording.
Only one recording?
Only two.
Do you remember the songs?
No. I don't write down no tune; just go ahead and play and get them over.
Getting back to Dizzy Gillespie and the musicians who were playing the other kind of music, about 1945, how about the other trumpet players? What did Red Allen think of Dizzy's playing?
Red Allen, if you want to know the truth, he didn't think about nobody's (side of it at all.)
I know. I mean, how did he like the way Dizzy played?
That's what I'm talking about, not to copy Dizzy, no.
He always felt like he could play better than anybody else. I'm telling you what I know.
That's a good way to feel.
(NOT CLEAR - SOMETHING ABOUT Roy Eldridge.)
What was that about Roy Eldridge?

We were playing at the Metropole and Roy, you know how he comes in? He said, "I got something for you. Play this." (....) I said, "That's no musicianship. You shouldn't do things like that." So he switched to another cut 'Body and Soul'. "Play this; play that." Buster got mad and went home and I walked off too...
What about Charlie Shavers?
Charlie didn't care; he just played.
What was Red's impression of Charlie Shavers?
Same as anybody else's.
Cootie Williams too?
Everybody.
Hot Lips Page?
Everybody. Red think nobody can outplay him.
Did you feel that way about the trombones?
Never in my life. I never felt like that about no trombone player in my whole life. Anybody beat me playing, I'm happy. I laugh about it, get a kick out of it.
There's a whole area that I want to - while you were making all this money every week, there were a lot of musicians

who weren't making any money (they were out of work), who could play. I'm sure you knew many of them who were not working. Did you ever hear musicians talk about the things that were wrong, that they felt were wrong, why they weren't working?
Well, yeah, sometimes.
What kinds of things were they talking about?
Sometimes they would get together and they'd want to work. One said, 'He's trying to cut my throat,' you know, for a job, working cheaper and all like that. That was true; guys did do that.
Suppose there had been a time here in New York when all the black bands played in all of the hotels here. Is that true?
Say it again.
Suppose there had been a period here in New York in the 30's where all of the hotels downtown hired black bands. Is that so?
I don't remember that.
Not in the 30's? Like they would work in the Hotel Taft and Biltmore and all that?
No, I don't remember.
Did you never work in any of those hotels?
No, not steady.
But you did work them on occasion.
I played gigs, like that, not a steady job.
No, I never worked on a steady job in a hotel.
Of the musicians that were around, the ones who were talking, well, this guy's trying to cut my throat, did any of the black musicians ever talk about a situation of the white musicians -
Getting more?
JCH: Yeah.

Yeah, getting more work. The fact that there were a lot of white men involved in the music industry, like John Hammond - were there any black people involved that you recall that were able to get work for musicians and recordings for musicians?

Well, so far as John is concerned, I don't know, John isn't so prejudiced, but there are booking agents who pay white musicians much more than they would the Negro musicians and the Negroes would accept it. I've had people offer me jobs and I'd say, 'Huh-uh ... you pay me what you pay him and I'll play for you.' Of course if one will do it, another one will do it. As long as you keep yourself down, you're going to stay down.

When the musicians got together to talk about those bad things that were happening to their lives, what kind of things did you hear them say? I mean, would one musician talk about how so-and-so gypped him, how he made this record for this guy and didn't get paid. Did you hear stuff like that?
Sometimes you would hear remarks about different things like that. When I got out I didn't like to talk about music.
No, I don't want to hear nothing about it.
What was the general attitude of the musicians - not only yourself - towards John Hammond?
Whose attitude?
Musicians.
About John Hammond?
Right.
The ones that I know about, I never heard nothing bad about him.
What did they think of Joe Glaser?
A lot of people said he was no good, but you had to understand him.
Understand him how?
Well, he was going to bawl you out if you asked for a lot of money...
What do you mean a whole lot of money?
Just like when I came from Boston and Red wanted me to come back with him. So I called him up and told him what I wanted. 'Can't pay you.'
How much did you tell him you wanted? Do you remember?

... I say, you're going to pay me more than $250 a week. 'Can't do it.' I said, you don't want me. So I walked back in the office one day, he made me so mad. I called him up and his secretary answered the phone. I was broke; I wanted some money. So first the secretary wanted to know who was calling.

So I knew he was there. So she said, "He's not in." I said, "You damn liar, you sea hag!" So I went up there and I kept straight to the back. He said, "You're not supposed to walk in here like that." I said, "Well, she's not supposed to lie to me like that." I said I wanted some money. She said, "Will you please give him a check and let him get out of here?"
Joe Glaser was booking the band at that time?
Yeah, booking Red Allen.
So then he was handling Louis Armstrong and Red Allen?
Yeah, he always handled Louis Armstrong. So Louis made him what he was to be.
What was his relationship with Red Allen? Did Joe Glaser also like Red Allen?
He and Red got along pretty good 'cause Red admitted he was an Uncle Tom.
He admitted that he was what?
Uncle Tom.
That he was an Uncle Tom?
That's exactly what he said over at the Copper Rail in front of Buster Bailey and me... He said, "I'll admit I'm an Uncle Tom to make a dollar."
How much was Red Allen making a week?
I sure don't know. Of course the Metropole, they didn't pay much money over there, nobody.
You weren't making $250 a week.
No.
You were making $200 a week in Cafe Society.

They were paying $82 scale or something so I said, I'm not going to work for no scale. So I told Red, "You're the leader... I want your permission... to ask the owner for a raise [?] He said, "Higgy, how much money do you want?" I said, "$250 a week." He said, "O.K." And Red was standing behind me. This is the truth. He said, "Don't give him nothing. I'm the leader. Give him what I say." His exact words.
Did you leave the band for that?
No, I didn't leave the band...
Was it possible that you may have been making more money than Red? Would that make him envious? Or making as much money as he was?
I didn't make that much.
Do you have any idea why he didn't want you to make that much?
I sure didn't. He said, I'm the boss and that was just it. Give him what I say.
I wanted to ask you, who was doing arrangements for that band? Did you all have arrangements or did you all just -
No, we mostly had arrangements.
When you recorded the records you made with that band -
The same way.
The same way... Did you record any of your songs? Did you all work out any of the songs that you wrote?
No, not with him. I did my recording with the Louis Russell band.
You told us the first time we came that you had written four songs. Is that all that you've ever written?
Yeah.
Did you write any more than four songs? Is that all that were recorded or published?
No, they're published.
No, but I mean, that was all, just four?
Right. .....

I want to ask you, at that time that you were working with Red Allen - we know that you were a big star at that time, winning all the polls on the trombone - did you have anyone ever write any music for you, other people write music for you?
No.
Didn't Irene - she wrote a song for you...
Irene wrote a song for you?
Yeah.
What song was that?
I forgot what it was.
Didn't she give it to somebody else. It was supposed to be - was it Trombone Blues?
She belonged to the ASCAP. That's where I belonged.
Do you belong to ASCAP also?
I said I should be, but I didn't do that. I just didn't do it, period. ... They gave me a slip to fill out and I didn't do it...
She's collecting right now because with the movie that was just made -
Well I mean the government takes a chunk out of that.
'Goodmorning Heartache' is one of the hits.
Since 1929, I collect royalties.
You mentioned that. 'Give Me Your Telephone Number'...
... Sometimes you get paid in stamps... It's according to how they sell.

We've gotten a lot accomplished today. We talked a lot about your life work till about 1950, the 50's. Now I think it will just take one more sitting and we'll be able to go on up from there from the 50's up till now. Then there are just some general questions that are the things I was asking you, the feelings of other musicians, especially the feelings that your friends and the musicians from your era who played together felt about some of the younger musicians who came up after you, like you were talking about Jay Jay, and like how they felt about Charlie Parker and about the pianist Bud Powell. If you had heard there was a couple of trombonists who were around, you know, people like Benny Green. Were you familiar with Benny Green's playing?
He's O.K.
Well, what's wrong with him?
I don't see nothing wrong with him?
(LAUGHTER) Just the way you said that! Did you like the way he played?
Yeah, but don't steal my stuff and then put in the catalog that I can't play. He played it note for note but I caught him. He was playing here at ( ? ).
On 118th Street?
Yes. I went over there one night and I told him. I said, "I got you this time."
Were you living here at that time?
Yes. It was in down beat. He said that I couldn't play.
Benny Green said this?
Yeah, and copied the tune that I had written, the solo, you know. They had him to copy it and put it in the magazine.
Oh, really?
Yeah. He said, "I didn't do it," and I said, "That's your end."
Did you go over to Minton's quite often when you were living here?
No, I didn't like it.
You didn't like it over there?
No.
How come?
Too many junkies.
That's something that we didn't talk about. At the time that you were coming up and all of the time, I mean from the very beginning, did you meet - were there many musicians who smoked pot?
Were there many musicians who smoked marijuana?
If they did, I didn't know too much about it. If they did, you know, they would keep it away from me...
How about the song that you recorded with Louis Armstrong's band, 'Song of the Vipers'? Isn't that about pot smoking?
(He gave me ?) the first reefer ever I smoked. I smoked two; never do it again.
You smoked two, one right behind the other?
With Red Allen, Saratoga Club, he came in from Chicago. It was cold, so -
Anybody want a cup of coffee or something?
No thanks. We're wrapping it up.

We're about through now so we could stand a little coffee... So we had a floor show down there too. Boy, it was jumping, Saratoga Club. So Louis came in and he sat in with us from Chicago. So everybody knew he smoked, so I said, "Give me a puff." He said, "It don't take but five." So I smoked five. I smoked the whole thing. I didn't feel nothing - then. So we had to broadcast that night. I said, "Give me another one." I smoked a whole one. So the time came to broadcast. I had the first solo. I don't remember playing nothing yet, the only thing I was just walking on a cloud, man... That's true. You know if you're drinking and get high and you go out in the fresh air, you sober up. Cats (...) gave me a steak and I ate it and it didn't

do no good. Went upstairs and stood out in the cold - no good. They brought me a pork chop down. That didn't do no good. I didn't do nothing but laugh. I didn't get straight until 1 o'clock the next day. I said, no more.
How did you feel?
I didn't have no feeling. Just as light, just like walking on cotton, just feel nothing.

When you mentioned about all of the junkies around Minton's and whatnot, how about the music that they played? Teddy Hill was the manager of the club at that time and that was an old band buddy of yours. Like you say, you were living right here, right up the street.
Yeah, but I don't know, I didn't care too much about it.
About the music?
About the gang that goes in there.
How about the music?
He had good bands in there.
Did the bands become involved in any kind of religious movements during your time? Things like becoming Muslims and so forth? Do you know anything about that? Nobody was a Muslim?
Play the music right as they had or leave them alone.
Nobody was into any religious things?
Religious songs, that's all right.
No, I'm saying, the musicians, were they involved in
No, I don't know too much about that.
You never heard anything about that?
No.
Were they involved in any kind of fads?
I don't know about that.
What about well-known musicians that may have been hung up on drugs like heroin?
I can't see it. No excuse for it.
No, but I'm saying, did you know any musicians like in the 30's and so forth that were addicted, or in the 20's?
Yes, I did.
Were there a lot of them? Was it a common practice?
No.
More people drank than used -
Sure did.
Than used heroin or something like that, but there were a few that did?
They needed their whiskey.
What about people like Lester Young and Billie Holiday?
Billie was a sweetheart.
What was your impression of Billie Holiday?
I loved her. I started to help her start all over.
How did you help her?
got to the Loew's got to the place, she got on stage there, she got to sing

She would do more for me than she would for her father. She went right in 129th Street where we used to hang out, after hours, and she was drinking wine. You know, we'd sit back and the musicians play and sang... So I used to tell her - I talked to her all the time and I'd say, 'Billie, now don't drink too much wine because you've got to sing.....' She made me a promise that she wouldn't do it, and she didn't. She was just a good kid. Her stepmother was the cause of all of it.
Her stepmother? Did you meet her?
I sure did.
What was the first time you met Billie Holiday?
I met Billie Holiday when I first came to New York in 1929.
How old was she then?
Oh, I don't know. She was old enough to know right from wrong. I guess she was about 16 or 17, something like that.
Did she have a big reputation at that time?
No, not at that time.
She was just singing around New York?
Yeah.
She had just come here or something?
Yeah. A nice kid, very nice, all the time.
But she was drinking when you first met her?
Mm-hm, she was drinking wine, sometimes top and
bottom; she'd mix it like that, you know.
Was she into anything else, prostitution or any other -
Not that I know of. Never heard of it.
What was your impression again of Lester Young?
He was O.K. We made some recordings together and we played gigs together. He was quiet; he didn't do nothing but play his horn.
What about Lionel Hampton?
(END OF REEL)
T7 / T8
Tell me, did you ever recall your parents talking to you about your grandparents, or anything about your grandparents?

blocks.s: ANNA MAE ORANGE, SISTER OF JCH:
blocks.x: About our other grandparents?
Yeah, you say you knew -
I knew of my grandparents. I knew my grandmother and I knew my grandfather.
Did they ever talk of slavery play with you?
My grandmother did. She talked and played of slavery.
What kind of things did she -

She said her father must have been white because I think - she was born in slavery, I know that. She was so white they wouldn't let her work on the farm. They had her to work in the big house, she said, and they couldn't control her temper. She used to sew and they would tell her to do different things and she wouldn't do it and she would talk back to them.
I remember one time she told me they stitched up her lips.
Really? And you told us the same story?
She told me it.
She talked so much.
She wouldn't give in to them
I thought it was my aunt.
In that picture down the hall they could pass for twins. The last time I saw it, beautiful!
Did they ever talk about music?
No, nobody did.
