They'd talk about how they used to sing, you know, after they finished their work and go to the cabins and they'd sing, you know, and on the outside, clap and stomp. In the night time, you know, after the work was over. They even did that when I was coming up.
But I'm sure they had music because when we were born, even the oldest, we had an organ in the house, so there's always been music in the house.
Oh, yeah, brought an organ to ( ? ).
Yes, and we traded it in for a piano but I mean there has been music in the house.
There was a long time before we had any music.
Do you remember when we bought the first organ?
Yes, we used to have quilting parties and we would invite people from all around. They would come in, you know, the

women, and they would quilt and sing while they were quilting. Sometimes they could make a whole quilt in one night. After that they would have something to eat and sing, sing and clap. But there was no music then.
What about square dancing?
They had - what do you call it - Jew's harp?
Yeah, Jew's harp.
That's what they used to use; I remember that, and the harmonica, in those days, but there wasn't any organ. Seems like we were the first people that bought an organ in the neighborhood.
How about some of the brass instruments? Did you ever hear of anyone playing trumpets or trombones?
I never heard of it. The time I remember an instrument was when Jay C. came to New York.
You weren't living in Atlanta then.
It was in Savannah; Jay C. didn't have anything to do with that. That was another band...
Garnett played trombone when Jay was just a little boy. I think you were married and away then.
I left home kind of early.
When you left, you left from where?
From Social Circle.
From Social Circle, so that was before you moved to Atlanta?
Yes, before we moved there. You went to live with my sister. We had an older sister that was living in Savannah and she went down there to live with her.
There was two other sisters older, Stella and Emma. Jay, Walter, and Marion was at home then.

I used to hear bands in Savannah, you know, since I've thought about it. Had one good friend that was in a band. Blew some kind of horn, I don't know what it was, so that was the first time I ever heard brass.
Would you feel that Garnett kind of influenced Jay C. into wanting to play the trombone?

I'm sure he did, although he didn't want to because I really think that he was afraid that he might be a dropout in school. He didn't want him to do anything with his instrument but he was determined he was going to do it. He was in boarding school but we lived in the ( ? ) house just across from Morris Brown and he would come over and have his meals there most of the time. He would slip out of the school and come over to the ( ? ) house and get his horn and go to the Roof Garden. When he would come back he would come around to my window and knock and I would go and open the door and let him in. He was slipping in and out and my brother didn't know anything about it.
... I was looking through the scrapbook and I came across this picture of Billie Holiday. That's exactly where we stopped last time. You were telling us about Billie Holiday.
Yeah, she gave me ( ) to the High Hat in Boston. I think that's where it was.
Did you work with her?
No, we never worked together. We did down to Loew's
State; we did a week down there, you know, on the stage. (I had her make that out to Cricket.)
Oh yeah, I see. While you were working with Fletcher Henderson's band, you said Billie Holiday's father Clarence, was working with the band with you. You say he was a guitarist?
Yes.
Did he ever speak of Billie Holiday, his daughter Billie, before she was singing.
Oh yeah, sure. He was crazy about her.
You must have been playing with Billie somewhere because there's Fletcher.
Oh yes, there was Fletcher at 52nd Street at Cafe Society...
I also saw a picture of you and Benny Morton sitting together.
Benny Morton, trombone player?
Yes. Was he in the Fletcher Henderson band when you were with Fletcher at all?
Not long. No, let's see, what happened? Whose place did I take?... Claude Jones? I dont remember.
But Benny Morton wasn't in the band at that time?
No, we didn't work in the band together. Let me see, who worked in the band? Claude Jones started.
(NOT CLEAR)
Yes, but Benny Morton had played with Fletcher Henderson
also and I was just wondering if they were playing with Fletcher Henderson at the same time or at different times?
He had two trombones. He had Claude Jones and Benny Morton... He let Claude go and Benny and I worked together.

Oh, that's it, they did work together. I saw the picture of them too in the book and I was wondering if that was - ... You were also telling us yesterday a little bit of how you reacted to trombone players such as Jay Jay Johnson, Benny Green, and their style. You said that their style was a little too technical to suit you?
No, I didn't say they - I said Jay Jay.
Just Jay Jay. But did that apply at all to - because around that time a lot of the younger trombone players were using more and more...

I haven't heard anybody with the style of Benny Morton, because most of the time when he plays, he growls, but not like Tricky Sam growled. That was part of his tone; that's the way he played. But Jay Jay Johnson, that was nothing but just technician, everything is going-going-going-going, and you don't know what's happening. I didn't; maybe they did.
Did you know a trombone player by the name of Jimmy Cleveland?
No, no.
Jay Jay was one of the trombonists that changed the style of trombone playing.
That picture, that was made down to Jimmy Ryan's Sunday afternoon. We switched horns.
Switched mouthpieces and horns - oh no, kept the mouthpieces and switched horns.
Tommy Dorsey and Charlie Shavers.
Tell me, after 1950 you had mentioned that you had worked with Red Allen - the band with Red Allen during the 40's - and up until 1950 you all worked together. Did you all stay together after 1950?
No, we went back together...
You came to Cleveland. They left the Brass Rail in Chicago and he and Red drove to Cleveland.
I stopped in Cleveland and had my band there.
You stayed there and played at the Tijuana.
How long did you stay in Cleveland?
I don't know.
Oh, about 3 months.
And this was 1950?

1950, because my brother from Philly came over and played with them, played trumpet. You picked up this group though right there in Cleveland. No, the trumpet player came there and you picked the other boys up in Cleveland, didn't you?
Yes, all the rest of the guys.
Because that's when the Tijuana was really a beautiful place. All the big bands.
Then after you left Cleveland in 1950, you came back to New York?
No, I went to Boston, from Cleveland I went to Boston.
What was happening in Boston?
When I went to Boston I went to Wally's Paradise. That's on Mass. Avenue and from Wally's on Mass. Avenue, about four doors from there, I went to the Savoy.
With whom?
From the Savoy - you know that was kind of a ritzy club - and then I went to the High Hat. That was supposed to be a ritzy club there. Then I came back to New York.
But who were you playing with, he said? Who were you playing with in Boston? Did you have your own band?
I had my own band.
Who was in the band?
Who was playing? Oh, you don't know the guys. I forgot the names myself.
Rex Stewart was over there because I have the picture of one of them. You featured Rex Stewart in one of them.
Was that when you first came to New York, Jay C., you played with Duke Ellington?
No, this was in the 50's. I know Rex Stewart was over there, Jay.
Oh, that's right, I forgot. That's when I had my
band up in - yeah, you got a picture of him in there - up in the Savoy; and boy, that was a jumpin' band.
The Savoy in New York or the Savoy in Boston?
In Boston.
How many pieces were there in that band?
Rex was living up in New York... and I sent for him. He came down and played with me; and then I had John Fields, a white fellow, on bass. I don't know, it was just a good band, very good band...
Five people in the band?
Six.
So you and Rex -
Wait a minute, I'm trying to think of the rest of the fellows.
Was there another horn player?
Trumpet, trombone, John Fields on bass - I'm trying to remember. It's written in there someplace.
How about after that? That was 1951. What happened after you came back to New York from Boston?
From Boston? I came here and did several gigs. Who did I play with? Did I go with Red Allen, 'cause I stayed with you for a while.
You came from Boston about '55. You stayed in Boston quite a while.
Oh, really?
Yes, he was in Boston for quite a while.
For about 3 or 4 years?
Yes, 'cause you were there when my father died, that's how I know, then when my brother died. And then you came here - I think you played at the Metronome - I mean Metropole.
That was about 1955?
50 something... Margaret knows.
1956. He called me on the job.
I knew he was there quite a while. He was there when my father passed.
After you came back to New York from Boston, what were you doing in New York?
I did a few gigs down to Jack Christy's place, you know.
Second Avenue, Central Plaz a on Second Avenue. He's got a plaque back there that Jack gave him.
I think I went with Red Allen after then.
When you started working in the Metropole?
Yeah, I think that's the way it went.
And like you stayed in the Metropole from about '56 to about how long?
(NOT CLEAR)
What year did you go to France, Jay?
Oh, I forgot about that.
We went on a boat with -
Sam Price.
When the Pope died. I can tell you exactly when he went because his passport is right here... That's when he went with Sam Price on the boat. That's the year the Pope died.
Yeah, we didn't finish out the engagement on account of that.
(GENERAL CONVERSATION HERE - NOT CLEAR)
How long were you there.
About three weeks, in different places.
Then you came back to New York?
Yeah, I came back.
Isn't there a picture in your album, taken on the liner?
Yes, I saw the picture.

He called me up on Sunday morning, 9:30 in the morning, and the operator said, 'Queen Elizabeth wants to speak to you.' I said, 'Queen Elizabeth? You must be kidding!' But the way the operators tell you, it's a boat. So I said, 'Queen Elizabeth? I didn't know I was such a celebrity!' Then she said, 'Are you Mrs. Jay C. Higginbotham?' I said, 'Why didn't you say so at first? Why did you get me all excited thinking Queen Elizabeth was calling me?'
She has a date on there. Can you read it? - when he first went over with Sam Price. That's when he went over on the boat, because he went three or four times.
It was 1958. That's the first thing -
That's it, that's when he went on the boat.
Was that the very first time you were ever in Europe?
Yeah.
Where were you playing in 1958 in Paris, do you remember?
No, I don't know. We played so many different places. Some steady nightclubs and then we did shows for -
Sam Price.
Yeah. We played in Brussels; I wish I was still there.
How did they like the band, the French?
They liked it.
When you came back after your first visit to Europe ...

You know, that's the first time he ever voted. That's when Rockefeller first went in. I took him to the voting place myself. That's the first time he ever voted, he said, in his life, first time. You know I always vote. We went across the street and we voted. After he got off the boat, I waited two and a half hours for this man to get off that boat, 'cause you know they let the first class off first. They were traveling tourist and then the last ones gets off the last. I brought him down, we went to the school where we voted, and then I went on to work. I never knew you couldn't get off a boat in a hurry. ... Sam Price had you all traveling tourist and you know for weeks Jay was eating breakfast like this. (LAUGHTER)
Tell me, do you remember some of the musicians who traveled with you in Sam Price's band? Who were some of the musicians in the band?
trumpet
I forgot the trombone player's name. Doc Cheatham was one.
Doc Cheatham was in the band?
Yeah, and J. C. Heard. I got the pictures of all of them in there but I don't remember their names. I forget my name...
Where did you all work next after you came back to the States?

I think the band broke up. I did work another gig with Sam Price. That was a place about 53rd Street there and Seventh Avenue, a nightclub, you know, you could dance and whatnot. We stayed there for about two weeks. I did lots of gigs with him but I wanted to break with him. He didn't want you to drink; I cheated, called him all kinds of names. Wanted to know what kind of kindergarden was this. No drinking, no nothing.
He was with Red Allen on - was it Broadway?
They have that.
Yeah, Metropole.
And you went to Copenhagen after he came back from France, I know that.
When you came back from Europe with Sam Price - you stayed in Europe for about a month?
About a month. Maybe not, maybe more. I'm not sure.
Then you just started to work around New York some more.
He played at some of the colleges I think, somewhere.
in Massachusetts.

Colleges? Oh, yeah. I played practically all the colleges up there and that was the last date I played up there. Got sick of Boston. When you get up there, you get stuck. I don't care how much money you get, you just can't get away from Boston, it's not that easy. The last date I played I think was Dartmouth College and I just packed up my bags. I was coming to New York...
(SOMEONE DROPS IN AND THERE IS GENERAL CONVERSATION FOR A FEW MOMENTS.)
I wanted to ask you, what was the union like. When did you first join a union, 802?
I joined in March 1929.
They had unions back then?
They sure did.
What were they like? Everybody had to join, of course?
Oh, yeah. I was supposed to join in '28 but first then they would test to see if you could read, give you a piece of music and send you across the hall.
And all of the bands had to -
(END OF REEL)
- separate? It was all one union here?
All one.
White and black belonged to the same local?
They did a little fighting in there... Pinky I don't know if you know him. He was a drummer. So you know,
one musician is a Negro, want to be this and one want to be something else - boy, they had a fight down there one day.
And what happened?
Nothing. Nobody won and everybody won. So now they have the Negros working down there just like the whites.
But both white and black belonged to the same union at the time?
Oh, yes.
Did you know Kenneth Rodne? He's a union official now. He used to have a band, I think, back -
Petrillo was the president when I joined.
Petrillo was the president?
Yeah.
Did they enforce the laws very strict at that time?
Not like now, no, no, no.
The white representatives wouldn't come up - or did they have white representatives to come up to the Apollo and the Savoy at the time?
They didn't do nothing but kick back.
What do you mean by kick back?
You were supposed to get so much. Like if you had a job playing in a theatre you were supposed to get $100 a week. They gave you $100 and said, but you got to give us back $25.
Who would say that?
No, that's the way they did then.
I mean, you would have to give it back to the band-leader? The owner of the club? You had to give the money back to the club owner?
Give it back to the club owner.
So in other words the club owner was reporting that you were making the scale but the fact was -

They would pay you the scale and you'd give the scale to the union. The union would give you your money and you'd take that $25 or $30 and give it back to the man that owned the place. But they caught up with Louis Russell and put a fine on him. Otis Johnson, trumpet player, said, "I'm not going to give back nothing. I played for that and I'm keeping it." So we had a trial board and they didn't fine Russell or nothing like that. They just called him the black sheep of the family... He apologized in a hurry too. Otis Johnson didn't give back no money but two-thirds of the musicians in New York working then, they kicked back, what we called it.
Yeah, the kickback, right. Was that even the practice at the Apollo and the Savoy?
Anywhere. No, not Savoy and not the Saratoga Club.
What about the Apollo?
Yeah.
They had kickbacks there?
Right.
What were the agents like that used to book the bands, like for instance Joe Glaser and the other agencies, William Morris and Alexander and all that kind?
They would try to get you money and whatever they would get, they would give it to you. They would see that you get it.

But did they ever try to do things like use double contract? In other words, like a double contract would be, if I wanted to hire you and Jimmy was your agent, then I would write a contract to Jimmy and Jimmy would write another contract to you. So if at first I'd say, "I really want to pay you," and Jimmy said, "Jay C. is worth a thousand dollars," so I'd give him a thousand dollars. He tells you the job is for eight hundred dollars. Understand?
I understand what you mean.
Was there a practice like that?
I don't know about that.
You probably were never that much involved...
Did you hear any musicians talk about that happening to them?
That kind of practice. Did they ever talk about that thing being - happening?
No, I never ran into it like that.

What were people's impressions of people like Joe Glaser? You've mentioned something about it, I mean the fact that - oh, before I even do that (make a note of it) - do you know anything about the relationship between Louis Armstrong and Joe Glaser?
Yeah, I know they liked each other. I know he paid him. Louis Armstrong didn't make all that much money when he first started.
He didn't?
I know how much he made.
How much did he make?
He made $750 a week when I first started with him.
That was for the entire band, or for him?
For Louis Armstrong alone... in Washington, D. C.
What year was that?
That was the first year I played with him, because we played the Howard Theatre. I will never forget that. I thought he was making two or three thousand dollars.
You don't know what year that was, do you? Was that in the 30's?
The first year I was playing with him, whatever year it was. 1929
That was in the 30's.
We had chorus girls. You know we all traveled together in the bus.

That was after Louis Armstrong had come back from Europe. Did they ever talk about the contract Louis Armstrong was supposed to have signed with Joe Glaser for a certain sum of money for the rest of his life each week?
Never heard of it.

He talks about it - I mean he admits it but I was just wondering, I had heard that the figure was somewhere like $1000 or $1200 or something like that a week for the rest of his life - that he was supposed to have signed in 1932.
Well, it could have but I didn't know anything about it.
Louis Armstrong obviously never said anything bad about Joe Glaser.
I never heard him.
He never cussed him out, they didn't have a bad period when there was -

No. I never heard him swear but once, twice. That was when he was going to meet his wife one night... The next time, he bought her some new luggage... The valet went to pull down one of the bags and he snagged it. I never heard nobody swear like that in my life. (LAUGHTER)
Which wife was that?

..... The stage manager - we just drove in, so he told Louis - Lou was swearing like mad - so he told Louis to shut up. Boy, you should have heard the names that Louis called him... When he get angry, don't bother him.
Did he fight?
He did that once.
But could he fight?
He did that morning. We came in - you know sometimes
he and I hang out like this. We had been out, you know, sporting around. It was too late for his wife. She threw a cup of coffee.
Which wife was it that you're speaking of? He was married three times. Which one?
Alpha. She died out in California.
Did he ever talk about his life or anything at all? Did he say anything to you?
No, not to me.

You say that he was a pretty strong and outspoken man. One of the things that maybe you can help to correct: you know, a lot of people of the younger generation looked at Louis Armstrong as being an Uncle Tom. How would you feel about that?
He is an Uncle Tom.
How so?

How so? How can anybody be one? Just an Uncle Tom, period, he and Red Allen. He worked and he got his money, but he didn't go around and say, yes sir, and you know, things like that. He didn't do that, no.
Why would you say then that he was an Uncle Tom?
I don't know how to explain it.
But you just felt that he was?
I know he was. (LAUGHTER)
The people were correct in saying that?
Red Allen was the same way. I told you that. He admitted it.
I'll tell you an incident but don't put it on tape.
O.K., go ahead.

...... Not only that, our soloist and our set was the first Negro band to open at the Strand Theatre downtown... During the intermission, you know you walk out in a little fresh air, there was a cop on the corner. Bill Robinson walked up, put his hand in his pocket, and gave this cop money, if I'm lyin'. I hope I'll never play a note. The cop said, "What is this for?" He said, "My name is Bojangles."
Just like that? He gave the money away?
And then Otis Johnson, you know, the trumpet player - boy, Otis was a killer. He can't gamble, if he play cards if he lose, he want to fight. Another time you came to Connecticut -
Hartford, Connecticut. That's what I tried to tell them but you shut me up. Midge Williams?

So he wanted his autograph. Sunday morning I think it was. So he always carried this pistol, a gold pistol. So a kid, he just asked, can I have your autograph please. He took out his pistol and started fighting. He shot up in the air and he whipped that kid over the automobile that was parked outside...
This happened in Hartford, Connecticut.
What for?
Nobody knows what happened. Nobody knew whatever happened because when we got to the cafeteria... Jay had to go
out on a little errand. So Sid Catlett and I were sitting in the restaurant. We were waiting for our train to come in. I'll tell you who else was up there was Rogers, the comedian.
Will Rogers?
Timmy Rogers.
He was there -
I was with Timmy Rogers a couple of days ago.

Yes, Timmy Rogers was up there. There was a whole lot of them up there. So anyhow, I went up to the cafeteria to get a sandwich and Bill Robinson came up and there was a white man standing there. He was high and he fell up against me. So nobody was paying Bill Robinson no mind. So he going to make a big splash - (BELL RINGS) - that's my kids.
The worst one - never in my life - I never hate nobody. People I don't like, I pray for them, but I can't stand this - every time I look at him I want to fight him so bad just one time.
Tell me, all of these things like you're talking about Bill Robinson and things about Louis Armstrong - did any of these things have any effect on your playing?
Yes, some of it did.
What kind of an effect?
(THIS IS NOT CLEAR AS PEOPLE ARE COMING IN OR LEAVING.)
Anyway, I think I was at the restaurant counter. Jay had gone on an errand. So Sidney Catlett and I were sitting at the table and I ordered a sandwich and Jay came back.

We were getting ready to make the train back to New York. So Bill Robinson comes up to the place. There's this white fellow. He was high. Well, he, you know, knocked up against me. I didn't pay him no mind. So Bill Robinson said - you know we were youngsters then, very young. So he said, "Is this man molesting you?" Nobody had recognized Bill Robinson, so he's going to take it out on me to be recognized, and that's what I didn't like and neither did Sid Catlett. I said, "No, he's not molesting me. The man is just high and he fell up against me." "Oh, I'll take out my gold pistol," and he did take it out. He had a gold pistol. So Sid Catlett came up to him. He said, "Now listen, let Margaret alone. Let her come on back and sit down and get her sandwich and let her alone." Somebody told Jay about the incident. We all got on the train coming back to New York. So he came over and he begged my pardon, he really did. He said, "I'm sorry." I said, "But you didn't have no business to make me, you know, make a fool out of me so you could be recognized." ...

I said, "Why pick on me; I'm nobody." ... When Jay heard about it we had to quiet him down... "Why did you pick on Margaret to make yourself famous?" He was already famous; he didn't have to do that to me.
because he was going to whip on everybody.
He was just going to make a spectacle -
Out of himself and make me look like a fool. We were all up there for fun, Tim Rogers and all. Even Tim Rogers remembered the incident. He may not remember me, but he may
remember the incident. Midge Williams - did you ever hear of Midge Williams?
She was the vocalist with Louis Armstrong's band.
I think she died very young.
Butch, I think they called her Butch. She used to call me Newly all the time.
I never will forget her, very cute, petite and cute. She died I think up in Detroit... She was so nice. In those days, you know, everybody was so nice.
JCH: Detroit or Chicago.

Tell me something, I read an article not too long ago that said that Ethel Waters was accepted more by the whites and she was a refined singer and she was a better singer. They were all trying to imply that Ethel Waters was a better singer than Bessie Smith.
Sure she was.
Yeah, in my opinion she was.
But did Bessie Smith appeal more to more people?
She was a down home blues singer.
Did she have much more mass appeal than Ethel Waters, I mean as far as black people were concerned?
Yes, but I knew about both, but I was never a jazz buff, (SEVERAL VOICES AT ONCE)
I didn't care about either one of them...
But the thing is, did Bessie Smith have the appeal, the mass appeal of the black people though?
Yes.
In other words, Bessie Smith was really more representative of the people than Ethel Waters.
During that time I don't know no Negro singer could sing like Ethel Waters and had the personality and still got it, that she's had ever since I've known her.
What about Ella Fitzgerald?
She's a doll. She's O.K.
But would you classify her with Ethel?

Sometimes she gets off. I caught her off twice we just had a little taste in Copenhagen, but nobody was playing then... She slipped just a little bit but she never slipped too much. But Ethel Waters, I just love her.
What about Mamie?
Mamie?
Mamie Smith?
She was all right. I made a record with her too. Right here in New York, we made three recordings for different studios with Fletcher Henderson.
What the big difference between Mamie Smith and Bessie Smith as far as their sound was concerned?
I can't answer that. They all sang the blues... I was a kid when I heard them; I used to sneak out of school. You know, when you'd get through singing they'd throw a quarter on the stage.
Do you remember when Bessie Smith died?
No, I don't.
The musicians didn't talk about the circumstances or the things that happened when she died, Bessie Smith died?
No, I don't hear it.
Did you have some kind of friendship all over among the musicians, I mean like if something happened would everybody get together and discuss it or something like that?

I think, in my opinion. Now if I'm wrong, I'm sorry, but I have friendship with all musicians, all, all. One I kind of resented; I told you who he was, but that was nothing. That doesn't mean a thing. People are jealous sometimes. Talking about Jay Jay, you know. But that doesn't mean anything. I like him just like I do other musicians. The only guy that had a little head on him was Johnny Hodge's.
Yeah, he's kind of rough to get along with.
Kind of rough up here in the head, had a big head.
Tell me, did the musicians ever get together and did you have any kind of a club or anything?
You mean a special club? No, you could just find a place to hang out and go and take your horn and sit down and laugh and talk, play cards, drink whiskey...
Didn't you used to have jam sessions?
Sometimes they would last until 11 or 12 o'clock the next day.
Didn't you also hang out at a place called the Turf?
That's where I met Billie Holiday. Don't you remember me telling you?
This girl that you ( ? ) on Prospect Avenue ( ? ) You came to my house. on ( ? ) Avenue.
Piano player.
Who was that?
His name is -
This was a lady, and you went to play with her, to have a jam session.
Hazel Scott or Mary Lou Williams?
No, I never played with - ... Wait, I'll get this chick straight here.
We'll forget about that.
No, we don't forget it. I mean, it's tough to remember all these things... Didn't she live in your building?

May have been. She lived under you. That's right, now I got you covered. I forgot her name, 'cause I used to take my horn and go in and play with her, sure did. She died; you told me she died, didn't she? ... Yes you did, you certainly did. I'll never forget it.
What was so significant about that? What was the important thing about this?
Nothing... Just like a lady that lived down on the next floor - she's blind but she can play anything you want to, anything.
What was her name?

She played in church. Name is Mamie, that's all I know. I don't care what tune you played, the only thing she'd say is, what key, and play. They are very dear friends of ours, especially the lady that Margaret lived with, Minnie - you know Minnie. Minnie, that lived on the next floor? We played for a birthday party down there, and she played too. I think she played in a church practically every Sunday...

The way you're speaking about this friend here, did many of your friends, musician friends, get together in a friendship atmosphere like that, when you didn't get together just to play with each other but just to talk. To jive with each other -
Nothing but piano and trombone, that was all.
Outside of that, were there other occasions where the musicians used to come - remember the Turf?
Turf Club?
Yeah, down on 49th and Broadway. Everybody used to come down there just like guys used to go to the Union Hall. But did the black musicians have a spot where they used to hang out by themselves?
No, I don't know about that.
Do you remember across the street from the Metropole when they used to have the -
The Copper Rail.
Right, but didn't everybody used to come and meet there at one time?
never heard I don't remember anybody going there to play.
Not to play, just to talk... to hang out.
Yeah, they go in there to hang out. Sure, white and the Negros.
When they were hanging out in those places -
No discrimination, everybody just laugh and talk. All musicians meet in there, white and Negros.

Jay C., what I'm trying to get at is like, in my home town in Detroit we had a musician's club as kids. We used to have a little society where we used to gather and discuss about music and problems. If some club owner wasn't doing right we'd black-ball him as musicians, say don't do this, don't work over here, don't have nothing to do with this person. Did you have anything like that?
Mm-mm-mm - no. I don't remember.
They had it but he -
You mean in New York?
He's talking about Detroit. In New York?

A social club, a social type thing... Like at the Metropole you said the guy would pay the band $100 to the union, pay them $100 and send the money over. You'd get your $100 and then go back and have to give this guy, the owner of the club, $30 kickback.
That's wrong, I knew that a long time ago.
What I'm saying is, now, things like that the musicians spoke about. Did they ever say, well listen, you know, like you
better watch out for this guy because you work in his club and you have to give him a kickback?

No. That left about 20 years ago because, see, you have your scales. If they hire me and the Metropole was open and I go in there, this comes from 802. I have to report to them first and they tell me the scales, how much tax I have to pay each week, and that's what I have to pay. If I don't make but a dollar and a half a week and they pay me a thousand dollars a week, they can't take out but a dollar and a half a week, and the rest of the money goes to me.
You still a member of 802?
Oh yes, they'll bury him... You know the kickback that he's talking about, when Freedom Land first opened- you remember Freedom Land -
Up in the Bronx?

Yes. There was a fellow that played down on 52nd Street, somewhere down there. He put a band up in Freedom Land with Jay and a couple other musicians. He was the one that got the kickback... He put another drummer up there instead of himself. What's his name?
I don't want to remember the name. Here's a guy trying to hold down two jobs. So they hired me to open, you know, to take the band up there. I was the first one to take a band in Freedom Land.
What year was that?

1958... This drummer had his job but he thought he could sleep and play up there and play on his job too, but they caught him. He sent another drummer to play in his place. He didn't play, but he sent someone else to play in his place.
Jay C., what about companies like Irving Mills, the music publisher?
You can have them.
What was he like and who was he?

He's a big publisher. I got his name on a record back there. I haven't been paid for it, haven't collected for it. I will if I take time. Any record you record, just like when I was with Lucky Millinder's band, if you want to make a record you write a tune. This is your tune. So the leader says, O.K. Got your arrangement and everything? After the record is printed, you look on that record, you see by Irving Mills and so and so and so. I got a record back there to show it.
Irving Mills, you said that he would put his name on the song, every song. Would you get any money from it? About how much from each record?
I don't know. You get a percentage according to how the records sell.
Did he give you a contract?
Yeah, they give you a contract. About the only way you're going to get it recorded is you have to let him put his name on that.
Did you ever do anything for him?
I didn't get anything from him yet, but I am.
But do you have a contract, a document?
I have it now.
You got a piece of paper from him?
I'm not in no hurry. The longer I wait the more I get.
O.K., what about this? You said that he used to sign his name on - did he ever actually publish his music in sheet form?
No, I've never seen that in sheet form, not on a tune that I had written, but I have seen it on lots of others - "Written by Irving Mills"... Or Sidney Mills, one of the two.

Sometimes they used to do things like - Thelonious Monk's Around About Midnight has three names on it - Cootie Williams as a bandleader, the publisher, and Thelonious Monk. Would that also happen with Lucky Millinder, like say, would it appear "Lucky Millinder, Irving Mills, and Jay C. Higginbotham"? Would the band leader take it, a share of it?
I don't know about it. I don't remember but two names on records.
The reason why I asked you is because early you said that Lucky Millinder and Red Allen had taken some music from you.
'Ride Red Ride'. So the thing was that they didn't give you any credit whatsoever for it.
Not a quarter... And I couldn't do nothin'.
What other companies - was Edward B. Marks doing things like that?
I don't know him.
What other companies besides Mills - was Mills the only one -
They're the worst you've ever seen?
Were there any other companies like that?
Not that I know of.
Was Irving Mills the one that was handling most of the black musicians?
Yes. White and the Negro.
The pop music and stuff?
Yes. There's a book - you saw the trombone book in there.
No, I didn't see the trombone book. I want to see it. Trombone Book of Jay C. Higginbotham Solos, published by - ?
It's small. small book.
Yeah, but by who?
I think it's by Mills.
So that he just like had the whole field like W. C. Handy, Duke Ellington, and everybody belonged to Mills.
Something like that.
Leeds.
Oh, Leeds, yes Leeds, I apologize.
Was Leeds buying up music, black musicians' music.
Black or white music. I know they was buying it.
When did this appear?
This? I don't know. Dates on it.
In the 40's? 30's?
In the 30's. We were working out with Lou Armstrong. We were working down in the Cotton Club when that happened - '39.

He wasn't involved in other things - I remember now, Leeds used to put out band arrangements. Like 'String of Pearls' and stuff like that by Glenn Miller and so forth. Did Glenn Miller get his stuff from Fletcher Henderson? A lot of people said that Glenn Miller was just a bigger orchestration of Fletcher Henderson.
The only thing that made Glenn Miller popular is Joe Garland when he wrote 'In the Mood.'
That's what happened?
Yeah, that made him the most popular band.
What year was this?

I don't know. I was in Lucky Millinder's band then. He wrote 'In the Mood' and he wrote 'Leapfrog', Joe Garland did. He wrote 'Leapfrog' after he wrote In the Mood, but 'In the Mood' made him rich and today you can't make nobody believe that Glenn Miller didn't write 'In the Mood.' Glenn Miller didn't have nothing to do with it.
How did he get it from Joe? If he just copied and made an arrangement of it. But he said that he wrote the tune? Glenn Miller claims that he wrote the tune?
Glenn didn't. I mean that's what the public thinks.
What about Tommy Dorsey and what was your impression of Tommy Dorsey and Glenn Miller? Did you think much of them?
I don't know nothing about (vulgarizations?) but they both are very nice guys.
How did you like their playing?
I think it's good. I know Tommy's good.
Was it jazz?

Both of them? Not too much. (LAUGHTER) No, that's right, because it's written down now. One O'Clock Jump, must be the first record when we started making these All Star records. I had the One O'Clock Jump and Tommy had the Bugle Call Rag. It's all written down in that book; you'll read it. He says, long as I play trombone I will never sit next to Jay C. Higginbotham and take a solo..and he had a whole quart of Grand Bad.
That was Tommy Dorsey?
Yeah.
What about Glenn Miller? Did you have any -

No, I don't know that much about him. Never had a conversation with him. I met him when we were playing in the Savoy. You know we had the opposite band. We just say hello and shake hands and call it a day.
Glenn Miller was at the Savoy Ballroom?
Yes?
When was this? It must have been sometime in the 30's no doubt.
It was early.
Early 30's? Did you mean they had white bands up at the Savoy?
Sure they had white bands.
These were white bands playing for almost black audiences?
Playing for anybody. Sure, they'd dance together, just like you walk and talk in the street today.
Not too many white went up there though.
No, there wasn't too many whites, but the white people would come up there.
Would you say there were 10% white?
I'd say around about 10%, yes I would, maybe more.
What other white bands? Did Benny Goodman appear there?
I don't remember.
What about Tommy Dorsey? Or what white bands do you remember playing up there? Paul Whiteman?
No, Paul Whiteman wasn't there.
At the Savoy?
We played downtown together.
Where was this?

Across from the Roseland when it first opened. I told you that the other night. The Beer Barrel Polka came out. Just in front of the Roseland, just opposite, one on one side and one on the other. And they had two bands.
Did any of those white bands in the 30's hire black musicians?
Sure.
Did Tommy Dorsey have black musicians?
He had Charlie Shavers.
In the 30's?
I don't know what year but he used to feature Charlie Shavers.
What about Glenn Miller?
I don't remember that. He didn't need nothing but what he had, because he had the best band there for a white man, playing the kind of music he played. He was just fine.

Would you say that out of all the things that was happening during the 30's, your band and the bands that you handled, Louis Armstrong - do you think that it should go down in history, is it really correct in saying that Benny Goodman was the King of Swing -
No.
Why not?
You mean the King of Swing as of now?
That's the way it reads in the history books.
Benny Goodman couldn't touch Artie Shaw.
Then you wouldn't agree to the historical interpretation that Benny Goodman is the King of Swing?
As of now, yes.
You say he is the King of Swing?
As of now. I think so too. There's too many clarinet players.
Was he more important to the clarinet than Buster Bailey or Albert Nichols?
Yes because I'll tell you one reason why, because Benny was white and he got more publicity.
I'm asking you, do you feel that Benny Goodman was more important than Buster Bailey?
No, never!
You think Buster Bailey should have been the King of Swing?
Tops on everything.
In bands which would you say - when they say the King of Swing, they're also saying that his band was the best band and the swingingest band of the 30's. Is that so?
Whose band is that?
Benny Goodman.
According to you, who had the best or the swingingest band during the 30's?
Small combination or just band?
Big bands and small combinations?
I'll tell you one - Fletcher Henderson. Let's see, who was the other one?
The band that you were in with Fletcher Henderson?
I don't know if I was in the band then or not, but I know he had the band.
What about small combinations?
John Kirby.
What about McKinney's Cotton Pickers?
Great.
How would they compare to -
Very, very good.
Would they compare almost on the same level -
Yes, with any other big swing band. They were from out of Detroit.

Well, how did the musicians feel now, all of these musicians that we've mentioned, the Fletcher Hendersons, the Buster Baileys, when all of a sudden they heard that Benny Goodman was the King of Swing? You never got together and talked about that?
Well, the public decided -
Not the public, the musicians.

No, not too much. Musicians don't talk about music much, very few, very few musicians. What I mean, the ones that I talked to. I don't about the others but the ones that I talk to, we don't talk that much about music. Sit around and gossip and have a taste and call it a day.
But things like that never came up, came up like about some of the inequalities, say that for instance that here is
Benny Goodman or Glenn Miller making all of this money. How come we don't make that kind of money?
How come who don't make it?
Some of the black musicians? Or were they making just as much as the white musicians?

Brother, that's a million dollar question, because they're white and we're Negro and they just feel that they are supposed to and we are climbing now. In 10 years from today Negros will be making as much money as the whites.
But what did they say then?
Then - they just figured that the white man was supposed to make more money than the Negroes.
The musicians felt that?
The white musicians.
But how about the black musicians?
They didn't think it. They were glad to get what they could.
Why?
Why? Because they wanted to work.
It was that bad?
They weren't that bad; they were that good.
I'm saying the times were so bad that they would work for a certain amount of money that somebody wouldn't say -
Times weren't bad then. That's when times were good. Times are bad now. (LAUGHTER)
I won't argue that point, a point well taken. But they never complained about things like that?
Yeah, they complained. Sometimes they had meetings. That's why they had meetings down at the Local 802. They brought the scale up and put things even.
What do you mean by put it even?
If you're a musician, you play, you deserve your money, you get the scale, you get your money, you call it a day. One as good as the other. If you can't make it, shame on you.
I don't understand. If you had a union and if the union is making scale, if the scale is set, why is it that there would be an argument as to one musician making more money than the other?
Well, why does the president make more than the secretary? He's the top man.
But this is for all, black and white.
You can't compare them together but somebody's more than somebody else.
But it wasn't a thing divided among race lines, that the black musicians were making less than the white musicians? That's the point I'm trying to say.
That's the way it started, when I came in.
They were complaining because the white musicians made more than the black musicians?
That's exactly what they did.
Who was leading - who started inciting all these people to think like this? Was it anybody in particular or everybody just felt that way?

I mentioned one but you don't know him. He's a drummer, very good drummer, name was Pinky ( ? ). That's when Local 802 was on Lexington Avenue because I went over there to join. They was fighting about who wanted to be who or whom. Fighting about the president and the secretary and he was fighting the president. We lived in the same building in the same street as Fletcher Henderson, Pinky Bujimi. He's a Negro drummer and a very good one too and would fight anybody anytime. He'd say, we're entitled to it just as much as you are. We play just as much.
What was the white argument. What did they say?
Oh, brother, take me about 20 years to tell you.
They just had every excuse under the sun, huh?
You know, they want to win. I'll put it like that. But the biggest majority of the time white people will win but they're not going to continue to win. I don't think so.
They win in that particular instance?
Any instance when it comes to music.
They just dominated the field.
Musicians are playing music now, Negro or white. used to
What about radio. When you/do radio shows and things. Was that common practice? Did you play often on radio?
No, very seldom you'd see a Negro on television unless he was playing an Uncle Tom part, valet or what do you call these guys sweeping up, taking up garbage -
Custodians, superintendent. But tell me when blacks weren't playing the radio shows, didn't they broadcast from the Savoy and all those places?
You got me now. Let's get out of the movies.
No, not movies, I'm talking about radio. Didn't you play radio shows that had live broadcasts from the Savoy and places like that?
Oh, yes. We had 30-minute sessions, something like that.
What would they pay?
I don't know, different prices.
But they did pay?
Oh, yes, you got your money.
And there were no blacks playing music for movies, or were they?
No, there wasn't anything like that. Because when we go in to do something it's written down or either they tell us -
Yeah, but didn't black orchestras or bands play for movies? Do you know of anyone that did?
Didn't Louis play for movies sometimes?
Nobody was making pictures, no, never did.
I say Louis - Louis Armstrong was doing it when you all wasn't working.
Oh, Louis did, sure. I know it. I've seen that several times.
Your band wasn't working but Louis was working.
... Louis Armstrong, Maxine Sullivan... 'Goin' Places' with Bing Crosby.
But not the rest of the band? The rest of the band never appeared or played the score or anything like that in the movies?
The whole band?
No. They wouldn't have a chance to do that. If they did you couldn't see nobody but the band, but they would have the music behind.
Did you make the music behind?
No, I didn't.
What about the theatres and things downtown? Were any black musicians playing then?
I played so many.
In the shows downtown?
Yeah, shows.
In the theatres.
They had the chorus girls then.
And pit bands and things like that?
White and colored.
Did they have mixed bands?
Yeah.
They played at Loew's State.
When was that?
He played Loew's State in New York. He played the Strand in New York when Josephine Baker used to come over.
Played the Paramount Theatre. Played all the big theatres in New York, all the theatres.
Pit orchestras?
No, they were on the stage.
But what about the orchestra that sat below, the regular musicians that stayed there. Like Broadway musicals.
(SEVERAL VOICES AT ONCE)
Were any black people playing in the pit orchestras? In a musical show downtown where they had an orchestra playing, black would they hire any jazz musicians?
Very seldom. I haven't seen a Negro yet in the pit and they keep a band now all the time and then they have a band on the stage. We played on the stage.
You remember the guy that said, 'Charlie, open the door?' He played at the Strand Theatre.
'Open the Door, Richard.'

He didn't get famous until he was almost ready to die. He played at the Strand Theatre, that I know. When Jay and them was playing at the theatre or even in the pit, Josephine Baker would come over to New York. She was the entertainer and there would be quite a few entertainers, white and colored.
Why would they use Josephine Baker?
They didn't just use Josephine Baker. They had Buddy Rich.
We played together out in Chicago. and she was doing the same act
They sat in the pit. Then they got so they sat on the stage, back of the performers.
You're talking about the orchestra used to be in the pit and then it moved up on the stage? But did they have black musicians in the pit?
They had black musicians at the Strand Theatre.
In the pit?
They had black musicians at the Capital Theatre. They had black musicians at the Loew's State Theatre, 'cause I was there.
What about at the hotels and things in downtown?
You wouldn't have made it so good. Harlem was the best place for you to live in those days. You couldn't live downtown so good.

You know this is a question, the reason why you can understand and then maybe you can tell me. In most of the interviews and things that I have dealt with with black musicians, they always talk about white people came to Harlem. But they never said anything about black people going downtown. Now could you go downtown?
Sure you could go downtown.
Sure. They didn't have nothing to offer.
Leslie Uggams, I met her. She may not remember me but I met her. She was dancing at that club downtown... That's where Louis Armstrong first met Lucille. Jay, you should know that.
I'm the one that introduced them...
It was the Cotton Club in those days and then it became the Latin Quarter.
That's down on 48th Street?
On 48th Street, right around the Metropole.
Was that the only club where they had black entertainers?
No, but all the black entertainers at one time was up in Harlem, white and colored. I have been in Small's with Lana Turner.
What did they have downtown then?
Nothing.
They didn't have big clubs downtown?
Everything was uptown.
The night life was uptown?

That's right. We had Sudan Club. I used to work with clubs. I used to get charity. We took care of the hospitals and everything. I was the treasurer of the club and everything. That's before Jay and I ever got married. I know a lot about Harlem. I can tell you more about Harlem than anybody in the world. I came here in 1932... This house, we had doormen, we had elevator men. They didn't allow you to walk up

these stairs. We had everything. But I can tell you the time I met Lena Horne. I can tell you I've met Lana Turner and I knew Ella Fitzgerald as a babe. She was only 15 years old. They don't remember me and I don't want them to remember me, 'cause I worked for a man that even gave Bob Hope his first tuxedo... I'm saying that you can meet these celebrities when they're not nothing and then when they get something they forget about you. You know what I mean? Now I knew Lena Horne down in the village, Cafe Society.
Tell me, Jay C., you were in Europe in the same year in 1958. You were in Europe?
I wasn't in any Europe in 1958.
You said you were in Europe with Sam Price.
I think the first time he went over was '56.
In Sweden?
Don't you have a '56 and two.
'58 was the first one?
I think we were on the same tour together.
That's when the Pope died.
Yeah, we were on the same tour. You went to Brussels, did you? And you went to ( ? ). In other words you played like a big gambling place.
That's when I got a whole busted hand.
... You were in Brussels, right?
Yeah, you were too, weren't you? I bet you loved it.
So you were in France. You were in Paris because I see that you have a stamp from Paris. What did you do, catch the
train into Paris? 'Cause it says Paris Nord Gare, that would be a train stamp..... But you stayed 3 weeks... In 1962 you were in Denmark, Copenhagen. (RECORDING NOT CLEAR)
(INTERVIEWER, JAY C. AND WIFE DISCUSS VARIOUS PEOPLE MET IN EUROPE.)
Don't you remember the singer you met over there?... He met Josephine Baker too.
She came to see me.
Was this in 1962 we're talking about?
'58 you say you met Josephine Baker... It's another colored singer lives in Europe. She's very famous.
You were also in Sweden. You were in Stockholm... Was it a concert in a park there?
We had three bands.
Was it open air?
No, it was just in a building. I don't know the name of it.
Was it a place that had a band on one side of it and then had a band on the other? It was like a dance hall?
Yeah.
And it was upstairs or something like that?
I think it was on the first or second floor.
What three bands?
I don't know. Played with this band a night, this one the next one, didn't make no difference, 'cause everyone of them played.
..... a colored singer.
Was she a jazz singer?
She's been over there quite a while.
Do you know the type of music she was singing? Do you have any material from his European trips?
Her name sounds like Nolan. She used to be in America. She was an American singer once and she used to write him. It looked like it was Noltin or...
When was the first time you went to Europe? '58?
You got his passport there.
I've been back about 4 times since then.
That was the first time you'd ever been to Europe?
When he went with Sam Price on the ship.
How did the people, you know, receive - the last time you were in Europe in 1962, how did they like you and the band?
They said they liked it.
He didn't go with the band, darling, he went by himself.
No, I went with Sam Price.
No, the last time.
When I went to Denmark...
How long did you stay then?
The last time he stayed two months.
That was in 1962?
... He's a personal friend of his, John Darville.
A manufacturer, very wealthy young man.
You stayed two months?
Trombone player.
He does it on the side, 'cause I talked to him. He called me -
Did I show you his picture?
He called us on the telephone.
The one I was showing you last night.
Yeah, you mentioned -
His picture's right on the dresser.
When you came back to the United States in 1962 what were you doing, what did you do?
From Denmark? I wasn't feeling well. That's when I had the gout, I think. Yeah, I think that's when it was.
But he's been back to Europe since.
I know. This time now, 1962, when you came back you said you had gout and were sick for a while. How long did you stay sick?
Off and on.
Were you able to play.
I didn't play.
He was real sick with a toe infection. He had a very bad toe infection. That's the first time he was really bad.
Nothing but needles.

That's when they thought he was going to lose his foot. Do you remember when we had the blackout? The year we had the blackout, my neighbor took care of Jay till I got home. The blackout went out five something in the afternoon.
That's when he had a heart condition.
Oh yeah, that's when you were here.

I stayed downtown 'cause I couldn't get home. When I got home 8 o'clock in the morning, 7 o'clock in the morning, I called my doctor and I got him right into Harlem Hospital. About 11 o'clock I had a bed, I had everything for Jay, 'cause I had a very good doctor. He stayed in there one month and two days. That's when he had a heart condition. Since then he's been up there three times.
But the gout is what got me.
Was this the first time that you had had any kind of serious illness?
Yes, when the blackout happened.
Before that his health had been -

Very good. I never will forget that blackout incident because I couldn't get home and the neighbor brought over a transistor radio for him. We didn't have one; we just had a telephone, that's all. Till 3 o'clock when the lights went on, where I was sleeping. I couldn't get home so they said, 'Margaret, the lights are on.' I said, 'I ain't going out here no three o'clock in the morning.' So I got home about 7 o'clock. The neighbor was looking out for him, that's one thing I'll say about these neighbors. They're still looking out for him. Then I got him in the hospital. It was his heart. Then he went in the second time; it was his throat.
When was the second time?
I mean, a couple of weeks after, a couple of months after, a year? After you got out of the hospital from the heart condition, were you doing any playing?
No -
He went to Europe.
I went back to Denmark. That's when I stayed so long, wasn't it?
You stayed two months.
Lived on a lake.
I'm confused. I thought he was just coming back from Europe when he had his heart condition.
No, he had his heart condition first.
You're speaking about the last time when he went to Europe in 1970.
He stayed two months... You're much younger than I am; I can't remember... All I know, he had the heart condition when the lights went out. You remember the lights went out in New York?

Yeah, I have that one. I want to find out what playing you've been doing since you came out of the hospital that time when you had the heart condition. I know you went to Atlanta in 1966 to do that record, 'Higgy Comes Home', with Bud Freeman and all of your friends down there. I know after that. But in 1966 you went to Atlanta to do that record. Your friend had sent for you, Lowenstein.
Yeah, I went there twice.
Bud Freeman and I went down to record and then I went back and played on a steady job.
For how long?
I think it was two weeks. Then I played the Jazz Festival.
The Atlanta Jazz Festival?
Yeah.
Who booked those things for you?
Joey Green. (George Wein)
Have you done a lot of work for George Wein?
And how, oh brother!
What were some of the things that you've done with him?
So many I can't tell you. All through Boston and didn't charge him nothing.
How do you mean didn't charge him nothing?

I just liked him that much, he and his whole family. I just felt like I was in the family. The last time I played in his house Mary Lou Williams was out there. Boy, it was cold, not c-o-l-d but k-o-l-d. So after we finished working we went out... That was the last time I went out there. I saw Mary Lou a couple of times...
After you did the record in Atlanta and you came to New York and you went back down to Atlanta to work on a steady job. Where was the place you were working in Atlanta on a steady job?
After I finished in Atlanta I went back to Social Circle.
Went back home?
Went back to the farm. Stayed down at my sister's about 8 days, right out in the country.
That was in 1966? What sister was this?
When did Sweetie die, Annie May? About 4 years ago. It was in the Fall. That's when he went back for his sister's funeral... He made 'Higgy Comes Home'.

After he finished making it, he came back to New York, right? Then you went back to Atlanta to work a steady job? Oh, for his sister's funeral, O.K., fine. Now, when you put together that record, 'Higgy Comes Home', you and Bud Freeman flew down from New York.
We did that. Bud came back -
Sweetie died.
Was that a lot of fun doing that record?
Lots of fun.
That was around Christmas time because on the record you recorded 'Jingle Bells' also.
It was before then because we did the same tune I played in the Newport Festival, 'St. James Infirmary'.
Was that you singing St. James Infirmary?
Yeah.
Did you do much singing in your career.
That on the record.
Now from there, in 1970 you went back to Europe. Who did you go to Europe with in 1970? It's in your passport, the last time that you were in Europe.
The last time I went it was with John Dow.)
Oh, again, two times you were there.
He sent for him. John (Dow) always sent for him.
He never went with a group. His sister and I took him to the airport, his sister over there. He filled in for what's-his-name, was supposed to go and he was sick and couldn't go...
Who was that?
Who was the musician that couldn't go and he sent for you to fill his place? When you went one time to Europe, when they sent for you? Who was the musician?
Sent for me?
He couldn't go. The other musician was sick and couldn't go so you went in his place, Jay. Who is he?
I don't remember that one. I don't remember nobody sending for me but John Hammond.
I said this musician could not go because he was sick. But you didn't stay long. Oh, I know his name and I can't call it.
We'll think about that. No problem. When you went to Europe this last time, how long did you stay about?
I stayed about 6 or 8 weeks.
It's on his passport.
And you worked pretty much the whole time you were there? You didn't have any time off?
Yeah, I did pretty good.
Working as a single, by yourself?
No, with the band. See, they had their own band over there. They featured me in the band. Just playing whenever you get ready.
Do you remember about how much money you were making a week?
I made a little.
A little bit or a lot?
They say it's a whole lot over there.
How much is a whole lot over there?
Now you're talking. I made it all right. All expenses paid, all the food, and I had my little bottle, didn't get drunk and did my work, period.
So after you came back from Europe that time, in 1970, what have you been doing since then? I know last year you played on the Newport Jazz Festival here in New York City.
I haven't played a gig since. I didn't feel like it.
Have you been sick?
I was sick then. I was so sick I almost fell on my face.
For Dickie Wells, he filled in for Dickie Wells.
Arvid Meyer Band
Dickie Wells was sick and couldn't go so Jay filled in for him. That's his name - Dickie Wells.
We played during intermission down here at the Festival. Benny Morton was on it. Just as I went to move I started to go down and he grabbed me and he grabbed my horn...
So you haven't been doing any playing. Have you been playing at all?
I've been out of the house twice since then. Tried to sneak out yesterday, wouldn't let me go.

Tell me, since you've been sitting in the house and thinking about a lot of the things that you've done in your life, what are some of the things that you back on and you say, "Wow! That was very exciting."
I do that.
I know. What things that you look back on are very exciting, like do you recall times working with Louis Russell or with Fletcher Henderson, what?
Yeah, they're all good. I don't remember nothing bad about no band I played with, no band. Every band I played with, I enjoyed myself.
Is there any one band that you enjoyed playing with any more than the others?
Louis Russell.
Why was that?
I don't know. Everybody was full of fun and everybody played. They loved to play.
Was it musical or social reasons that you -
Both.
Both reasons that you enjoyed working with Louis Russell. That was the time that Benny Goodman and some of the white players were doing a lot of stealing?
Practically every night.

You mentinned a couple of times ago that Benny Goodman was coming up and at that time he couldn't play jazz at all, but a little later he was beginning to get it together. How did the black musicians feel about Benny Goodman and the rest of them coming up and stealing?
They didn't mind.
They didn't mind?
No, they loved to play. They said, let's play this and see. Try to pick up on this.
How did they feel -
When you got competition you go more. Everybody knows that you are best...
How did they feel about it later on when Benny Goodman was making a lot of money playing the things -
They're not going to tell you.
But they didn't like it?
They loved it. That's where they got their money from. They came in here and copied what we played.
How did the black musicians feel about Benny Goodman making a great deal of money, becoming very famous -
They didn't mind. I didn't hear nobody squawking. We liked it.
(NOT CLEAR)
You sit down and play. You listen to a musician, 'Hey, man, let's put a couple of notes on there. See if we can catch up with this.'
And they did catch up with it and you say the black musicians were happy to have Benny Goodman steal their phrases from them?
There's no other way. You can't take it away. If I hear you play, you cannot stop me. You in the other room and I'm in here listening. You can't stop me from listening.
Didn't they feel that they should be making this money instead of Benny Goodman?
I don't know how they felt.
Maybe Mrs. Higginbotham can tell us something about that.

I can tell you an awful lot about that. I used to go to the Savoy Ballroom every Sunday in my life when I was a youngster. I didn't miss a Sunday. He and Chick Webb, Sidney Catlett, Walter Johnson, Sammy Williams - we had two bands at the Savoy Ballroom, you know. I was young...you all weren't even born then. We had two bands at the Savoy Ballroom. Jay was in the Chick Webb band and then there was another band which I can't remember. I even told them. I said, 'These white musicians are not up here for nothing. They're up here for a reason. They're up here to steal everything they can get. Benny Goodman was one of them. 'Cause I met him, he sat at the table and drank
with me and everything. He wrote down everything these kids would write - would play.
How do you mean that? He wrote it down as they were playing?
He wrote down their music.
I know, but as they were playing?
That's right... Well, they thought it was great because a white man came up there to listen to them.
They weren't aware that he was taking...
No, they thought it was the greatest thing that the white man came to listen to them. You don't have to take my word. You can take all of my friends' words...
We were playing something that they couldn't catch up with.
But didn't they catch up with it? They caught up with it financially, though, didn't they? Didn't you feel anything about that?

I was married to him and I was out having a good time. But I told Walter Johnson - he was a drummer - you know, we always sat at a table together. I used to tell them, these white people are not up here for no good. They stole every thing, but they thought it was cute for a white man to be up there listening to them play, you know, they thought it was cute. When you know anything, Benny Goodman stole everything.
You said that Harry James was up there, and Tommy Dorsey.
All of them... sitting right there at the Savoy Ballroom.
And all the musicians felt that way. They thought it was a cute thing, huh?
I wouldn't call it cute. We just played and didn't give a darn and if you can catch up with it, that's up to you.

You see, I wasn't supposed to have no good sense. I was just about 22 or 23 years old. I wasn't supposed to know what it was all about. But I knew what they were doing. I used to tell Walter Johnson and Sidney Catlett and all of them that these white musicians ain't up here for no good, no good, and they stole everything! But they never could steal Jay's style, but they stole everything else. Even Chick Webb. Chick Webb and I were the best of friends. He used to say, "Why do they come up here?" Benny Goodman
What did Chick Webb say about that?
He died soon after.
Chick didn't give a darn. The only thing he wanted to do was get on that bandstand and play.
Now this was the feeling of most of the musicians?

I'll tell you, kids, /...The Negro they had (the sound) both to stand in the bottom and the stopper their hands and they let the white man take it away from them. Now I'm telling the truth, 'cause I was here and I was there, but they couldn't steal everything. They never could steal certain styles, but they could steal most styles.
Did you ever hear Tommy Dorsey playing his stuff, that you feel he took from you?
Playing what?
The ideas that came from you.
I haven't heard him play like nobody but himself.
You know what made Glenn Miller famous?
Miller, and that's why I love him.
Did you ever know what made Glenn Miller famous?
Joe Garland made Glenn Miller famous, with In the Mood.
We were talking about that.

Joe Garland wrote it; Edgar Hayes played it. Edgar Hayes was the first musician - you know Edgar Hayes; he's my girl friend's husband. They live out in California. We all came up together. Edgar Hayes wanted to buy that music. When I lived down on ( ) Seventh Avenue he lived down there too, he and his wife. They all wanted to buy this music. He wouldn't sell it to nobody but Glenn Miller, Joe Garland.
He didn't sell it to Glenn Miller. Joe Garland is rich off of that tune today.
Edgar Hayes is the first one that ever recorded it.

Glenn Miller made the tune popular. That's Joe Garland's tune and Joe Garland is collecting the money and Joe Garland has got money like this and as long as he lives it's going to keep coming in every time he plays the record.
What about the so-called piano school of Harlem, people like Willie the Lion and Fats Waller and Albert Ammons?
They were the best.
What was that like? Did you work with any of those people? What about Earl "Fatha" Hines?
We played down at Cafe Society together.
I know Willie the Lion Smith; I know him very well.
Willie the Lion Smith - we worked - I don't know, can't anybody play with Willie the Lion. But we had three piano players, three boogie-woogies, down at Cafe Society.
There were one or two questions I wanted to ask you. One, what happened to the family estate, the farm.
Oh, my father sold it...
Are we all finished?
No, you're not finished. I'm just finished...
What about Count Basie? What did you think of his band and so forth?
He got the swingiest band anybody ever heard.
I mean what about it in the 30's?
I don't know that much about it.
What about Duke Ellington in the 30's?
I don't know that much about him.
What was Duke's reputation at this time?
The only time I've seen Duke was on the stage and we made two recordings together. I have never had a conversation with him, he nor Count Basie.

What about - I guess it will be my final thing - what about other forms of music, like for instance could you tell me what was happening like gospel and spiritual music... and what was the folk music like?
I like some folk music if you don't abuse it, but I don't know how to explain it. If you don't abuse it, it's beautiful music, if you don't abuse it.
Did you listen to any old blues - do you remember any in particular?
I listen to a whole lot of this noise I hear around here.
I'm talking about in the 30's and 20's and stuff like that.
Blues? You know, like Lonnie Johnson, guys like that.
You did.
Yes, somebody knew how to play the blues.
My final thing will be, what about the field of religious music, who were some great religious singers that you know?
I can't think of the name and I played for him. I made a whole lot of records for him too.
Who was the agent for black religious music, gospel and spiritual and stuff like that?

I know who you're talking about. The last time I saw him was down to the Central Plaza. I tell you one you might - maybe you won't like him but I really did - I don't know if you know Rosetta Thorpe. I don't care what Ethel Waters sings, I love it.
Oh, you mean Ethel Waters had something against Rosetta Thorpe?
No, you asked me one question and I'm answering another one. I finished with Thorpe and now I'm on Ethel.
What about classical black musicians. Who did you run into?
I don't know. I don't hear that much.
Do you know people like William Grant Still?
I don't listen that much...
What about Paul Robeson?
That's my man.
Roland Hayes?
You know of Paul Robeson?
Yeah, we worked together down at Cafe Society.
What was he doing there?
Singing.
What was your impression of him?
Very extra special good.
How did you feel about the way he spoke about what was happening to black people at that particular time?
Say it again.
How did you feel -
I didn't have too great an opinion because I hadn't heard all that many Negro people singing.
What about the things he said, his politics?
Oh, I know that's what you're thinking about... I knew that was coming. You don't like him because he went to Russia.
No, I love him, I adore him. I'm asking what is your impression of him? I like him very much.
I like him because of what he is. He did what he wanted to. He didn't bother nobody, he sang, he did his business, so that's the only thing I can say.
What about Roland Hayes?
Good, in my opinion.
Did you ever see him, hear him, or work with him?
I seen him and heard him.
Did you ever work with him?
I like him.
I wanted to ask you about some of the shows they were having during the late 20's such as "Shuffle Along". Did you catch any of those "Blackbird" shows of the 20's?

No. I was at school then. Yeah, because I remember when they came to Cincinnati. They came to Cincinnati in 1924 and I went to the theatre to hear them... Eubie Blake and Noble Sissle. After the show broke up then Eubie Blake and Noble Sissle came back to Cincinnati, just as a team. I went out to hear them
several times. They played away out in Cincinnati for the rich people. We'd stand outside and listen.
What did people think of Scott Joplin?
Never heard him.
The ragtime piano player.
Nope.
What did musicians think of Jelly Roll Morton?
Everybody said he's the only musician that really told the truth about musicians and what was going to happen.
How so?
He'd get on the corner and we'd listen every day. He would tell guys - and that was a long time ago - you wasn't even born - what was going to happen to musicians up until -
What did he predict?

No, he'd try to teach them music. He had a blackboard in the Rhythm Club and he'd try to show them music and would tell them what would be happening about 20 or 30 years from now. He didn't lie about nothing.
What were some of the things that he said?
Oh, I can't remember them.
Why did he pick the Rhythm Club?
Well, that's where all the musicians hang out... That's 132nd Street and Seventh Avenue. It's still there.
Up on the second floor?
No, it's first floor.
What kind of a club was it, organization was it?
They had a poolroom and then they had a blackboard up there and you could bring your horn in and jam.
They had piano in there?
And then you could gamble.
Had a piano and everything?
Oh, yes.
It was like a private club then?
It wasn't private. Open, anybody could come in.
Who opened the place?
Ray Howell. It was around the corner at first but it wasn't big enough. They had it in the basement then. It's still open now.
Do you know how it started? Did it start after you were in New York?
How it started? No, it was open when I came to New York.
And you just used to congregate there?
They changed it from downstairs, to upstairs on the ground floor. JCH and horn.

There was a question as to some of the things I've read and heard from other people that Jelly Roll wasn't always telling the truth. I heard statements - they said that he would have - he told everybody that he wrote everything, that he was responsible for every solo that everybody played and that he started jazz and the whole thing. Is that true?
That's what he said.

Let me tell you one thing. It's funny, Jelly Roll Morton used to tell jokes, you know. He said it take about 25 niggers to make a chinch. He said niggers ain't no good. Yes, he said it, and the musicians don't forget it today. He didn't lie much. He said it'd take 25 niggers to make a chinch. (LAUGHTER) He said it, he said that.
Why would he say something like that?
He had that diamond tooth up there. He didn't care, and he was talking and pretty near everything he said it came out pretty near right.
Would you say that he was responsible for jazz?
No, I wouldn't say nobody was responsible for jazz because I don't know how jazz started.
Did it start in New Orleans?
I don't know. I don't believe it did. I don't know where it started. I don't have the slightest idea.
There was a professor -
That's how people say.
But you don't go along with that theory?
No, but I had to go along that night because I got $800 for saying it.
Where was this?
In New Orleans.
They told you to come down there to play and say something?
...They had a concert down there.
You went along with the idea -
This was where it all originated.
You told them, you're right.
That was my script to read.
Who wrote your script?
I read the script.
Who gave you the script?

The producer. We had a program. We had Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong and Jay C. Higginbotham, and the rest they had the house band. You do your solo. They gave you a script to read. That's when they changed - was it Bourbon Street? It was another street. Q: Beale Street?
And changed it back to Beale Street or Bourbon Street. It's been the same street ever since - Bourbon Street.
What did you think of Sidney Bechet?
I loved him. You did too.
at course. Did you ever encounter things that they write about in the history about Creole musicians opposed to the other black musicians?

No, never. I don't know nothing about no Creole black musicians or nothing. I just know about people. 'Creole Lady' - name of the tune, that's about all I know. Chicago music and New Orleans music and all those kinds -
Kansas City?
I was playing jazz music before I heard any jazz music from New Orleans or Chicago, 'cause we had a Graphonola.
Wind it up and play the records. That's the way I - you know.
Where were the records from that you were listening to?
I don't know the names. I remember one...
That was a composition played by a jazz band?
Wasn't no jazz music to me. They was just playing.
Who recorded that?
I do not know. My sister bought a Graphonola, not a Graphophone. You'd just buy your records and put it on there. The bulldog was listening.
What about the cylinders? Do you remember machines that used to play the records that were cylinders. The records weren't on discs but they were on a cylinder.
No, I don't know anything about that. The only one I know you wind up -
Like the old Bluebird labels and all those things.
Yeah.
There was a professor at Howard University that said that jazz didn't start anywhere particularly, it was just happening all over. Eubie Blake told me the same thing.
I agree with that!
Eubie Blake told me that he heard jazz in Baltimore, Maryland, in 1900. Do you go along with that?
Yes I will. I just got through saying that I didn't know nothing about no jazz music from New Orleans or Chicago jazz.
They didn't talk about regions of jazz or jazz centers or stuff like that?
Say it again.
They didn't have jazz centers or something like everybody said, let's go to New Orleans 'cause that's where it come from?
No.
They never said anything about, let's go to Chicago?
They never said anything about it, never did.
They never said anything about going to Kansas City either?
No, never heard it, never did.
How did the church people look upon jazz music?

They didn't in the beginning because I remember when my sister was going to Atlanta University and they made a jazz tune out of some church tune and the president made some kind of speech about it. I was over there.
What did he say?
I don't even know the name of it, but the first religious tune, the biggest hit was When the Saints Come Marching Home. That's the only one I remember.
They didn't want you to play jazz?
No, they didn't want it then.
They didn't want you to dance?
No, they didn't mind you dancing but they just didn't like to hear church tunes, you know....
They didn't want you to jazz up the spirituals?
Jazz up the church tunes.
But they didn't mind the other?
No, play anything you want, dance. The "Saint" thing is the biggest thing that ever happened yet, in my knowledge.
Were any of the musicians into the Muslim religion or Islamic religion?
Beg pardon?
Were any of the musicians in the Islamic thing or Muslims or anything like that in the 30's?
Not to my knowledge.
Never heard of anything like that? Were drugs a problem in the bands? Dope?
Never heard of that. I never heard of no dope.
Things like heroin and so forth like that? Everybody was drinking at the time?
People drank corn whiskey.
And that was about it?
That was about it.
Do you remember telling me about Louis Armstrong giving you a reefer once?
He was talking that way before you were born.
