You told me Louis Armstrong gave you a joint, a reefer. He gave you some marijuana once.
Oh, yeah.
Somebody also had mentioned to me one time about Louis Armstrong and cocaine.

I don't believe that. Of course the way Louis acted, I don't remember if he was high, so help me God, if he was ever high - I don't remember seeing him high and I've seen him smoke reefer. I never seen him high or get out of place, never.
But you never started using anything like cocaine or heroin?
I don't believe he ever did. I don't believe it, I don't care what nobody says.
Speaking of Louis Armstrong, did you see his funeral on TV?
No, I didn't see it. I was too sick to look.

Peggy Lee sang The Lord's Prayer and there were a couple of other things like that, but he didn't have the New Orleans type of funeral... Do you think that he would have like to have had a New Orleans type funeral? Did he ever talk about the type of funeral that he might like?
I haven't heard of it, nothing.
Well, just from your knowing him, what kind of funeral do you think he would have -
Just by knowing him, the only thing I can say is he was just the greatest guy and he should have had one of the best funerals.
What would you consider to be a best funeral?
Just another funeral.
I mean like we have always had - when I say we I mean black people, we've always had, especially black musicians -
Color don't make no difference.
No, but I mean the musicians have had different types of funerals.
People like could go to the funeral and could get in ... and watch the casket go by, something like that.
How about the bands that played?
I figured they might have a band from New Orleans to play for him. But I don't know because I think I just came out of the hospital the day before or after. We were in the hospital the same time.
Have you ever thought about what you would like to have the musicians do in tribute to you?
No, hm-mm. Just say, well, he was a pretty good old guy. (LAUGHTER)
Tell me, how would like to be remembered?
And give him another drink! (LAUGHTER)... I don't know what's going to happen to me when I'm dead.
What would you like to see happen to you? Would you like to have one of your favorite musicians play a specific song for you or something?
No, no.
Would you like some of your music played at your funeral?

Well, that's kind of tough to talk about. I've been dreaming I was dying for the past two weeks... I mean that's the kind of pills the doctors give me, you know, hallucinations, you have everything like that, you know.
Jay C., a lot of the musicians have said to me, they used to get in trouble like with the police and things down South travelling. Did you ever get arrested or anything like that?

Musicians used to tell me that guys - it was easy for black musicians to go to jail for different things, like you're in a town or something, you know. Did you ever get arrested or anything like that?

No. Yeah, I got arrested in Decatur, Georgia. No, this was fun. You know we had the fire bells then. You know they have a large population now. So we were playing at night and there was a fire, so they rang the bell and we went up on the town to see which way the fire truck was going, three of us. Everybody ran but me and I was too stupid. I was too scared to run.
How old were you then?
Oh, I think around about 9 years old.
You never had any other problems like with the police or government or anything like that?
No... I don't get fresh with no cops and I don't have no problems with nobody. Sometimes, you know if you're in
a crowd and they say keep moving or something like that - I'm going to move.
The cops never arrested musicians for smoking marijuana and stuff like that?
They didn't lock me up for marijuana; I don't smoke.
I know - (LAUGHTER)
I wish they would, then I would sue the city.
Times like 1929, 1930 -
No, never... The only two reefer I saw in 1929, were the two I told you I smoked with Louis Armstrong...

Jay C., now that the ladies are out of the room, what did people say if they ever caught you with white women? What was the attitudes of the police and club owners if you had a white woman? Would you get in trouble like that?
If I had a lot of money?
A white woman.
What about a white woman?
If they caught you with a white woman or something like that, would you get in trouble for fooling around with them...
They didn't bother me in Lexington, Kentucky. They didn't bother me in Meridian, Mississippi. They brought me a quart of whiskey every morning.
Did she stay with you?
She didn't stay with me. She brought me a quart of whiskey every morning... Listen, if they see you with a white
woman in the South they're going to say, well I know she's got to be colored, because they could say a spook ain't got nerve enough to walk with a white woman in the South.
But did they do that? They did it, though, didn't they?
They didn't do it to me.
No, but I'm saying black men did go with white women in the South?
Sure. What's wrong with that?
No, but I'm just saying that they actually did and they thought you were crazy if you did.
You ever been South? Did you ever go with a white woman in the South? They didn't bother you, did they?
No, but I'm talking about 20 or 30 years ago.

That's what I'm talking about. I was with Fletcher Henderson and you know Bea. She's white as anybody - Fletcher's first wife. We played theatres there, Fletcher Henderson's band, and if we wanted a sandwich we'd have to go around to the back... She'd go right in front and get it.
Was she white?
No, she looked white.
Was that your mother?
No.
I don't know if you call it stupid, dumb, or what but I was just lucky.
A: ...shacked up four or five times, maybe more.
Who was his first wife?
You first wife was Lily Mae Marlene, wasn't it?
Beatrice.
Who was the second?

This is my second... I had more wives than Artie Shaw, but we weren't married. Common-law, but I was married twice. This is my second wife. First, second, and that's all. A million years, be right here together. That's the only thing that never bothered me, is color.
It never bothered you?

Never, when I was a kid on the farm, walking behind a plow, white colored never bothered me. Never did, and I went with white and colored and wasn't trying to show off or nothing. Nobody just bothered with me... I wasn't showing off.
I told you that you would be getting paid for this interview and I gave you the check for $2,000.
That's what I wanted to ask you.
What are you planning to do with that money? Do you have any ideas as to things that you would like?

I know what I'm going to do with it. I gotta have my teeth fixed and I've gotta get glasses. But what I can't understand is how you had it made out to Mr. and Mrs. I can cash a $5,000 check without my wife's name being on it.
The reason it was made out to -
No offense, just let me say this... She said the other night, I haven't finished reading your letter. I didn't know

how much money it was, because money don't bother me, never did. So she said, I'm going to straighten out this money business. So I didn't know what she was talking about. But when I look at it, I said, well this is nice. See, these got to be fixed and I got to get glasses. Now, you got Mr. and Mrs. Higginbotham. Now what she's going to do, cash it and tell me, I'm going to take this and there's going to be trouble. But there won't be no trouble. I'll tell you why. Just cool, everybody. There ain't going to be no trouble 'cause I got another check coming. I'll say if you want to take part of this, you take it and you won't get nothing in the next one, like that.

The check was made out that way because you told me that you hadn't been out of the house in a year and you couldn't get downstairs, so it was decided that the best way to do it would be to have your name and your wife's name -
I don't mind. That's
quite all right.
You see, that way you would have to sign it, endorse it on the back, and she would have to endorse it on the back before it was cashed.

I understand but I've given her plenty checks, you know, and haven't been out but twice. Just sign it, she cashed the checks. So I looked at Mr. and Mrs. and said, "What? I didn't know she was doing as much as me?" But it doesn't make any difference. It's in the family.
That's why it was made out that way.
Okay.
There's one more thing I wanted to ask you about and that was a little about what did you do in the Rhythm Club? You said they hung out there. What did they do when they were hanging out?

Just go in and say hello if you don't have no place to go. If you see guys sitting down playing cards, say may I get into and join, you know. Then sometimes they play poker and then they got a poolroom. They shoot pool, but no more music. They did have a blackboard there and the musicians would take their horns in there and one guy would write down something and see who could play it. That's when we were really having fun. Say, I bet you can't play this. You remember Charlie Dixon? He was an arranger. He could arrange tunes and boy, the notes that he would put up on the blackboard, you had to do a whole lot of reading. It was nothing but fun.
Were a lot of the musicians trying to learn to read better at that time?
No, they just went on and tried to read? What you can't do, you can't do.
Were they practicing?
No, the guy'd just write something on the board and say read it. Take you horn and go ahead and play it. And that was clean fun.
Was it becoming more necessary for guys to be able to read in the bands?
